knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be proper convex, let \(x,x^\star\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and suppose \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\). If \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\), then \[F(x)-F(x^\star)\le \varepsilon+\langle g,x-x^\star\rangle\le\varepsilon+\|g\|\,\|x-x^\star\|.\] Consequently, any verified bound \(\|x-x^\star\|\le R\) makes \(F(x)-\inf F\le\varepsilon+R\|g\|\) a computable certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient of norm δ certifies objective error at most epsilon plus Rδ when a radius R to an optimizer is known.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Subgradient Norm Alone Is Not a Scale-Free Value Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of geometric or growth information when converting a nonzero approximate subgradient into objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no universal function of \(\|g\|\) alone that bounds \(F(x)-\inf F\) over all proper convex functions and points with \(g\in\partial F(x)\). Indeed, for \(F(t)=\delta t\) on \([0,R]\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, at \(x=R\) one has \(g=\delta\in\partial F(R)\) and \(F(R)-\inf F=\delta R\), which is arbitrarily large for fixed \(\delta>0\) as \(R\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small nonzero subgradient does not by itself bound objective error; a radius, growth condition, or comparable scale is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta\in\partial F(R)\) while \(F(R)-\inf F=\delta R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternative-Based Status Certificate System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let data \(d\) determine two witness sets \(W_{\mathrm P}(d)\) and \(W_{\mathrm A}(d)\), representing a primary system and an alternative system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility systems for which an exact theorem of the alternative has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An alternative-based status certificate system is a pair of predicates \[\mathsf P(d;u)\quad(u\in U),\qquad \mathsf A(d;v)\quad(v\in V)\] satisfying, for every admissible datum \(d\), \[\bigl(\exists u\in U:\mathsf P(d;u)\bigr)\ \dot\vee\ \bigl(\exists v\in V:\mathsf A(d;v)\bigr),\] where \(\dot\vee\) denotes exclusive disjunction. A primary-status certificate is a witness \(u\in W_{\mathrm P}(d)\); an alternative-status certificate is a witness \(v\in W_{\mathrm A}(d)\). Validity therefore requires both disjointness, \[W_{\mathrm P}(d)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow W_{\mathrm A}(d)=\varnothing,\] and exhaustiveness, \[W_{\mathrm P}(d)=\varnothing\Rightarrow W_{\mathrm A}(d)\neq\varnothing.\] In optimization, the first witness commonly certifies feasibility or strict feasibility, while the alternative witness is a multiplier, separating hyperplane, or recession direction certifying the complementary status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternative-based status system consists of two explicitly checkable witness predicates. For every admissible instance exactly one witness set is nonempty. A witness from the primary set certifies one status, such as feasibility, while a witness from the alternative set certifies its mutually exclusive counterpart, such as infeasibility. Both mutual exclusion and exhaustiveness are part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(W_{\mathrm P}(d)\) and \(W_{\mathrm A}(d)\) is nonempty for every admissible datum \(d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining relation is \((W_{\mathrm P}(d)\neq\varnothing)\iff(W_{\mathrm A}(d)=\varnothing)\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas, Gordan, Stiemke, and Motzkin systems instantiate the definition with linear equalities or inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: A returned witness has a status interpretation that can be checked directly from the instance data.
The absence of a primary witness is converted into the existence of an alternative witness.
boundary_notes: Mutual inconsistency alone is insufficient; an exhaustive alternative theorem is also required.
Weakly infeasible conic systems may defeat finite strong-separation certificates and therefore require a refined status system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Theorem-of-the-Alternative Form
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each datum \(d\), let \(S_1(d)\) and \(S_2(d)\) be two explicitly specified systems of equations, inequalities, or cone-membership conditions with solution sets \(F_1(d)\) and \(F_2(d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical and mathematical form common to finite-dimensional alternative theorems; the actual systems and regularity hypotheses must be supplied by a concrete member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A theorem of the alternative is an assertion that, for every datum \(d\) satisfying stated hypotheses, exactly one of \[S_1(d):\quad u\in F_1(d)\] and \[S_2(d):\quad v\in F_2(d)\] is solvable. Formally, \[ orall d,\qquad  igl(F_1(d)
eq\varnothing igr)\ \dot\vee\  igl(F_2(d)
eq\varnothing igr).\] Equivalently, it combines weak exclusion \[F_1(d)
eq\varnothing\Rightarrow F_2(d)=\varnothing\] with the alternative existence implication \[F_1(d)=\varnothing\Rightarrow F_2(d)
eq\varnothing.\] In convex applications, \(S_1\) is generally a feasibility system and \(S_2\) is a separating or dual-multiplier system whose strict inequality makes simultaneous solvability impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A theorem of the alternative states that exactly one of two fully specified systems has a solution for every admissible instance. It contains two ingredients: a solution of one system excludes every solution of the other, and failure of the first guarantees a witness for the second. In convex optimization, the second system usually expresses separation through multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1(d)\neq\varnothing\) holds exactly when \(F_2(d)=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The assertion may be written as \((\exists u:S_1(d,u))\iff\neg(\exists v:S_2(d,v))\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas alternatives use nonnegative multipliers.
Gordan and Stiemke alternatives exchange strict primal positivity with homogeneous dual conditions.
Motzkin alternatives combine strict and non-strict inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: An alternative witness is a finite certificate of failure of the primary system whenever the concrete theorem guarantees exhaustiveness.
boundary_notes: The hypotheses establishing exhaustiveness are part of each concrete theorem and cannot be omitted.
An ordinary duality statement is not automatically a theorem of the alternative unless the two solvability claims are exhaustive and exclusive.

notation.meaning: Solution set of alternative system j for datum d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas-Type Separation Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be a convex cone generated by the feasible combinations of a system, and define its polar cone by \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear, conic, and constraint-qualified nonlinear convex alternatives represented through cone membership or global Lagrangian inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Farkas lemma family is the collection of alternatives having the canonical separation form \[b\in C\quad\dot\vee\quad \exists y\in C^\circ:\langle y,b\rangle>0,\] with sign-reversed polar conventions giving equivalent variants. Its members replace \(C\) by a cone or upper image determined by the problem data and express the separating functional through nonnegative multipliers. The linear member takes \(C=\{Ax:x\geq0\}\). A conic member takes \(C=A(K)\) for a convex cone \(K\), subject to closedness sufficient for strong separation. A nonlinear convex member replaces membership by the implication \(g(x)\leq0\Rightarrow f(x)\geq0\) and certifies it through \(f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)\geq0\) for every \(x\), with \(\lambda\geq0\) under an appropriate constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Farkas family consists of alternatives between representability in a convex cone or upper image and a strict separating functional. Linear, conic, and nonlinear convex forms differ in the object being separated and in the regularity needed to guarantee a separator, but each turns failure of a feasibility or implication system into a multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Farkas-type member has mutually exclusive primal membership and strict polar-separation alternatives, with hypotheses ensuring exhaustiveness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the dual cone \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\geq0\ \forall z\in C\}\), the alternative is \(b\in C\) or \(\exists y\in C^*:\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: For finitely generated cones, closedness is automatic.
Nonlinear convex Farkas statements require a condition such as strict feasibility or affine constraints with a relative-interior feasible point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A separator is an independently checkable infeasibility or implication certificate.
boundary_notes: If the relevant conic image is not closed, a point in its closure but outside it need not admit a strict separator.
Different sign conventions change displayed inequalities but not the underlying alternative.

notation.meaning: Polar cone under the nonpositive inner-product convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the systems \[Ax\le b\] and \[y\ge0,\qquad A^\top y=0,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\] is solvable. In the second system the strict inequality can be normalized to \(\langle b,y\rangle=-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system Ax≤b is feasible unless a nonnegative row combination cancels the variables and makes the combined right-hand side negative; exactly one alternative holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x:Ax\le b\) and \(\exists y\ge0:A^\top y=0,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\) holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Inequalities between vectors are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear systems; no constraint qualification is needed because the finitely generated cone \(A\mathbb{R}^n_+\) is polyhedral and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear Farkas alternative associated with \((A,b)\) consists of the systems \[\mathrm{(P)}\quad Ax=b,\qquad x\geq0,\] and \[\mathrm{(F)}\quad A^Ty\leq0,\qquad b^Ty>0.\] Exactly one of \(\mathrm{(P)}\) and \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is solvable. Equivalently, \[\exists x\geq0:\ Ax=b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(A^Ty\leq0\Rightarrow b^Ty\leq0\bigr)\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^m.\] A vector \(x\) is a feasibility certificate; a vector \(y\) satisfying \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is a Farkas infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a matrix A and vector b, exactly one of two systems is solvable: b is a nonnegative combination of the columns of A, or there is a vector y whose inner products with all columns are nonpositive while its inner product with b is strictly positive. The first witness certifies feasibility and the second certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists x\geq0:Ax=b)\ \dot\vee\ (\exists y:A^Ty\leq0,\ b^Ty>0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(b\in A\mathbb{R}^n_+\iff b^Ty\leq0\) for every \(y\) satisfying \(A^Ty\leq0\).
Changing \(y\) to \(-y\) yields the convention \(A^Ty\geq0\) and \(b^Ty<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), feasibility means \(b\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any Farkas vector rules out every nonnegative solution of \(Ax=b\).
Linear infeasibility therefore has a finite, directly checkable certificate.
boundary_notes: Replacing the strict inequality \(b^Ty>0\) by a non-strict inequality destroys exclusivity.
Free primal variables or mixed inequalities require a transformed but equivalent Farkas form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Conic Images Destroy the Strict Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closed-image boundary for the finite-dimensional conic Farkas alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(A:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(A(X)=(X_{11},X_{12})\). Then \[A(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is not closed. For \(q=(0,1)\), \(q\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\). Consequently, \(A(X)=q,\ X\succeq0\) is infeasible, but no \(y\) satisfies \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle q,y\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed semidefinite image has infeasible right-hand sides that cannot be strictly separated, so the unqualified conic Farkas alternative fails.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) with the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\), and infeasibility of \(A(X)=q,\ X\in K\) has no strict conic Farkas separator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Image Conic Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(b\in F\). Define \(K^*=\{s\in E:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility under the explicit closed-image hypothesis \(A(K)\) closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the conic image \(A(K)\) is closed. The conic Farkas alternative consists of \[\mathrm{(P)}\quad \exists x\in K:\ Ax=b,\] and \[\mathrm{(F)}\quad \exists y\in F:\ A^*y\in K^*,\quad \langle y,b\rangle<0.\] Exactly one system is solvable. Equivalently, \[b\in A(K)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y,b\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }y\text{ with }A^*y\in K^*.\] A vector \(y\) satisfying \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is a strict conic-separation certificate for infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the image of a closed convex cone under the constraint map is closed, either b has a representation Ax with x in the cone, or a dual vector y has nonnegative pairing with every representable vector but negative pairing with b. Exactly one alternative holds. The closed-image hypothesis excludes weak infeasibility at the boundary of the image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A(K)\) is closed, then \((b\in A(K))\ \dot\vee\ (\exists y:A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle y,b\rangle<0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual condition says \(y\in(A(K))^*\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), the result reduces to a linear Farkas alternative.
For self-dual cones, such as the positive semidefinite cone under the trace inner product, \(K^*=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict dual separator certifies primal conic infeasibility.
Closedness makes every infeasible right-hand side strongly separable from the conic image.
boundary_notes: The image of a closed nonpolyhedral cone under a linear map need not be closed.
If \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), neither primal feasibility nor a strict Farkas separator holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Without Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional failure of the nonlinear multiplier conclusion without Slater strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=\mathbb R\), let \(f_1(x)=x^2\) and \(f_0(x)=x\). The implication \[f_1(x)\le0\ \Longrightarrow\ f_0(x)\ge0\] is valid because its premise forces \(x=0\). However, no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies \[x+\lambda x^2\ge0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.\] Thus the multiplier equivalence can fail when no point satisfies \(f_1(x)<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The valid implication x²≤0 implies x≥0 has no global certificate x+λx²≥0, demonstrating failure without strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint implication holds, but no \(\lambda\ge0\) makes \(f_0+\lambda f_1\) globally nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear Convex Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Write \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear convex systems under either strict feasibility or affine constraints with a relative-interior feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume either \(\exists\bar x\in X\) with \(g(\bar x)<0\), or all \(g_i\) are affine and \(\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}X\) with \(g(\bar x)\leq0\). Then the implication \[g(x)\leq0\Rightarrow f(x)\geq0\qquad(x\in X)\] holds if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\) such that \[f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)\geq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Equivalently, exactly one of the following is solvable: \[\exists x\in X:\ g(x)\leq0,\ f(x)<0,\] or \[\exists\lambda\geq0:\ f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)\geq0\ \forall x\in X.\] Under strict feasibility, the set of such multipliers is also compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convex constraint qualification, nonnegativity of f on the feasible set is equivalent to the existence of nonnegative multipliers making the Lagrangian expression f plus lambda times g globally nonnegative on X. Thus either a feasible point violates the desired implication, or a multiplier certifies the implication for every point, but not both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([g(x)\leq0\Rightarrow f(x)\geq0\ \forall x]\iff[\exists\lambda\geq0:\ f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)\geq0\ \forall x]\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The multiplier set is \(Q^*=\{\lambda\geq0:\inf_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x))\geq0\}\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing affine \(f\) and \(g_i\) on the entire space recovers a linear Farkas lemma.
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiplier is a global certificate, not merely a local stationarity condition.
Under strict feasibility, the certificate set is nonempty and compact.
boundary_notes: Without a qualifying regularity condition, the implication may hold while no multiplier exists.
The strict inequality \(f(x)<0\) in the violating system is essential to exclusivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear convex Farkas multiplier existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and compactness of nonnegative global multiplier certificates under either strict feasibility or affine relative-interior feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\) and \(g_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,r\), are convex and \(f(x)\ge 0\) for every \(x\in X\) satisfying \(g(x)\le 0\). Define \(Q^*=\{\mu\in\mathbb R^r\mid \mu\ge 0,\ f(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}g(x)\ge 0\ \forall x\in X\}\). If either (i) there exists \(\bar x\in X\) with \(g_j(\bar x)<0\) for every \(j\), or (ii) every \(g_j\) is affine and there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(X)\) with \(g(\bar x)\le 0\), then \(Q^*\neq\varnothing\). Under condition (i), \(Q^*\) is also compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the convex function f is nonnegative throughout the inequality-feasible region, then a nonnegative global multiplier certificate exists under strict feasibility or affine-constraint relative-interior feasibility. Under strict feasibility, the multiplier set is compact.
assumptions_latex: \bigl[\exists\bar x\in X:\ g_j(\bar x)<0\ \forall j\bigr]\lor\bigl[g_j\text{ affine }\forall j,\ \exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(X):g(\bar x)\le 0\bigr]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q^*\neq\varnothing,\quad\text{and under condition (i), }Q^*\text{ is compact}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear convex Farkas multiplier existence and compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of nonnegative global multiplier certificates under either strict feasibility or affine-constraint relative-interior feasibility, with compactness only in the strict-feasibility case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f$ and $g_j$, $j=1,\ldots,r$, be convex and suppose
\[
\forall x\in X,\qquad g(x)\leq 0\Longrightarrow f(x)\geq 0.
\]
Define
\[
Q^*=\left\{\mu\in\mathbb R^r\mid \mu\geq 0,\ f(x)+\mu^\top g(x)\geq 0\ \text{for all }x\in X\right\}.
\]
If either (i) there exists $\bar x\in X$ such that $g_j(\bar x)<0$ for every $j$, or (ii) every $g_j$ is affine and there exists $\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(X)$ such that $g(\bar x)\leq 0$, then $Q^*\neq\varnothing$. Under condition (i), $Q^*$ is also compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppose the convex functions f and g_j satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 whenever x lies in X and all constraints g_j(x) ≤ 0 hold. The set of nonnegative multipliers making f(x)+μᵀg(x) nonnegative for every x in X is nonempty if either the constraints are strictly feasible at some point of X, or the constraints are affine and feasible at a relative-interior point of X. The multiplier set is compact only under the strict-feasibility condition.
assumptions_latex: \left[\exists\bar x\in X:\ \forall j,\ g_j(\bar x)<0\right]\ \lor\ \left[\forall j,\ g_j\text{ is affine},\ \exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(X):g(\bar x)\leq 0\right]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q^*\neq\varnothing,\qquad \text{and under condition (i), }Q^*\text{ is compact}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gordan–Stiemke Strict-Feasibility Alternative Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). Strict inequalities are componentwise. The family concerns homogeneous or affine systems whose primary condition requires strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear systems; the Gordan and Stiemke forms use different orientations and should not be conflated term by term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Gordan–Stiemke family consists of strict-feasibility alternatives generated by orthogonality and nonnegative cones. A homogeneous Gordan form is \[\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ Ax<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \{\mu\geq0:A^T\mu=0\}=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, exactly one of \(Ax<0\) and \(A^T\mu=0,\ \mu\geq0,\ \mu\neq0\) is solvable. A homogeneous Stiemke form is \[\exists x>0:\ Ax=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \{A^T\mu:A^T\mu\geq0\}=\{0\}.\] Thus exactly one of \(Ax=0,\ x>0\) and \(A^T\mu\geq0,\ A^T\mu\neq0\) is solvable. Affine extensions add right-hand-side pairings that distinguish strict from non-strict alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gordan–Stiemke family links strict feasibility in a linear system to the absence of a nonzero nonnegative orthogonal witness. Gordan places strict inequalities in the image Ax; Stiemke places strict positivity in a null vector. Each orientation has an exactly complementary homogeneous dual system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Gordan and Stiemke pairs are exclusive and exhaustive strict-feasibility alternatives.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For Gordan, \(Ax<0\) exists exactly when the cone of nonnegative vectors in \(\ker A^T\) is trivial.
For Stiemke, \(\ker A\cap\operatorname{int}\mathbb{R}^n_+\neq\varnothing\) exactly when \(\operatorname{range}A^T\cap\mathbb{R}^n_+=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: Gordan's affine extension replaces \(Ax<0\) by \(Ax<b\) and introduces the scalar pairing \(b^T\mu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The alternatives characterize strict feasibility and are useful for compactness tests of linear-program solution sets.
boundary_notes: Strict positivity cannot generally be replaced by nonnegativity without changing the alternative.
Matrix dimensions differ between the Gordan and Stiemke orientations, even when the same symbol A is used.

notation.meaning: Every coordinate of x is strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Status Certificates for a Conic Linear Optimization Problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone and consider \(\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), with dual \(\sup\{b^Ty:c-A^Ty\in K^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic linear optimization; certificate completeness depends on closedness and duality regularity and is not asserted universally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solvability-status certificate is a witness of one of the following forms. A primal-feasibility certificate is \(x\in K\) with \(Ax=b\). A dual-feasibility certificate is \(y\) with \(c-A^Ty\in K^*\). An optimality certificate is a feasible pair \((x,y)\) satisfying \[c^Tx=b^Ty,\] equivalently \(\langle c-A^Ty,x\rangle=0\). A primal-infeasibility certificate is a vector \(y\) satisfying \[A^Ty\in K^*,\qquad b^Ty<0.\] An unboundedness certificate is a feasible base point \(x_0\) together with \(d\in K\) such that \[Ad=0,\qquad c^Td<0;\] then \(x_0+td\) remains feasible for every \(t\geq0\). These witness predicates define statuses even when no theorem guarantees that one must be returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a conic linear problem, status is certified by directly checkable witnesses: feasible primal or dual points, a zero-gap feasible pair for optimality, a separating multiplier for infeasibility, or a feasible base point plus a cost-decreasing recession direction for unboundedness. The definition distinguishes validity of each witness from completeness of the overall classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed witness certifies its named feasibility, optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness status.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a feasible primal–dual pair, zero objective gap is equivalent to complementary pairing \(\langle c-A^Ty,x\rangle=0\).
special_cases_latex: With \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), these are the standard linear-program status certificates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every listed certificate can be verified using finite-dimensional linear algebra and cone-membership tests.
An unboundedness witness supplies the explicit feasible ray \(x_0+td\).
boundary_notes: Weak infeasibility may provide no strict separating certificate.
Primal and dual infeasibility can coexist in pathological dual pairs; the listed predicates alone do not impose an exhaustive trichotomy.
review_flags: No inspected source stated this exact unified conic status-certificate taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.title: Status Certificates for a Conic Linear Optimization Problem

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(\nu\) satisfying \(\inf_x[\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle\nu,Ax-b\rangle]>0\) certify infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), \(
u\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(\delta>0\). If \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle

u,\delta)\) is an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative inequality multipliers, equality multipliers, and a positive global lower bound on their aggregate constraint function certify infeasibility of the convex constraint system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of strict multiplier certificates under finite-dimensional closed residual-image separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated closedness assumption, exactly one of the following holds: \[(0,0)\in S,\] equivalently the constraint system is feasible; or there exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), \(\nu\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle\nu,Ax-b\rangle\geq\delta\qquad\text{for every }x.\] By positive scaling, the margin can be normalized to \(\delta=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the residual upper image is closed, infeasibility is equivalent to a strict multiplier certificate, whose margin can be normalized.

\(S:=\{(u,v):\exists x,\ g_i(x)\leq u_i\ \forall i,\ Ax-b=v\}\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint system is infeasible if and only if it admits a positive-margin multiplier certificate of the seed form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Farkas Infeasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and consider the feasibility system \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear equality systems with nonnegative variables; broader conic systems require additional closedness qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Farkas infeasibility certificate for \[Ax=b,\qquad x\geq0\] is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[A^Ty\leq0,\qquad b^Ty>0.\] Its validity condition is purely algebraic. Moreover, the system is infeasible if and only if such a certificate exists. Under the sign-reversed convention, the same certificate is written \[A^T\hat y\geq0,\qquad b^T\hat y<0,\] where \(\hat y=-y\). Thus the certificate strictly separates \(b\) from the finitely generated cone \(A\mathbb{R}^n_+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the system Ax equals b with nonnegative x, an infeasibility certificate is a vector y whose product with every column of A is nonpositive but whose inner product with b is positive. Such a vector exists exactly when the system is infeasible. Negating y gives the common opposite-sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\geq0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\iff\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^Ty\leq0,\ b^Ty>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(b\notin A\mathbb{R}^n_+\iff\exists y\in(A\mathbb{R}^n_+)^\circ\) with \(b^Ty>0\).
special_cases_latex: For inequalities, slack variables convert suitable systems to this equality-and-nonnegativity form.
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate is independent of any attempted primal solution.
Scaling a certificate by any positive scalar yields another certificate.
boundary_notes: A zero value \(b^Ty=0\) does not certify infeasibility.
For nonclosed conic images, infeasibility need not admit a strict certificate of this form.

notation.meaning: Polar cone of the column cone of A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-Direction Certificate of Linear-Objective Unboundedness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set and consider \(p^*=\inf_{x\in C}c^Tx\). Define \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization of a linear functional over a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recession certificate of unboundedness below is a direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) satisfying \[c^Td<0.\] For any feasible base point \(x_0\in C\), the ray \(x(t)=x_0+td\) is feasible for all \(t\geq0\) and has \[c^Tx(t)=c^Tx_0+t\,c^Td\longrightarrow-\infty.\] In this linear-objective, closed-convex setting, unboundedness below corresponds to the existence of a cost-decreasing recession direction. For a conic linear system \(C=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), such a direction satisfies \[d\in K,\qquad Ad=0,\qquad c^Td<0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession certificate is a feasible direction that can be followed indefinitely while strictly decreasing the linear objective. Starting from any feasible point, it generates an explicit feasible ray whose objective tends to minus infinity. For conic equality systems, the direction lies in the cone, belongs to the nullspace of A, and has negative objective slope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=-\infty\) corresponds to the existence of \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) with \(c^Td<0\); every such \(d\) explicitly certifies unboundedness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(C=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) with a feasible point, \(\operatorname{rec}C=K\cap\ker A\).
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedron, the certificate is a cost-decreasing extreme ray or a conic combination of recession generators.
immediate_consequences_latex: One certificate produces infinitely many feasible points with arbitrarily low objective value.
The zero direction can never certify unboundedness because its objective slope is zero.
boundary_notes: An unbounded feasible set need not make a particular objective unbounded below.
For nonlinear objectives, recession-function conditions replace the simple scalar slope \(c^Td\).

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper closed convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(f^\infty(d)<0\), then \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex unboundedness certificate using a feasible ray and negative recession value.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a nonzero direction \(d\) satisfies \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(f^\infty(d)<0\). Then \(x_0+td\in C\) for every \(t\ge0\), and the recession inequality gives \[f(x_0+td)\le f(x_0)+t f^\infty(d).\] The right-hand side tends to \(-\infty\) as \(t\to+\infty\). Hence the pair \((x_0,d)\), together with verification of the negative recession value, certifies that the minimization problem is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible base point and a feasible recession direction along which the recession function is negative certify unboundedness below.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Ex=h\}\] be nonempty. Its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad\le0,\ Ed=0\}.\] Then \[\inf_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle=-\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists d\in\operatorname{rec}C\ \text{such that }\langle c,d\rangle<0.\] This equivalence is asserted for nonempty polyhedral feasible sets.

children.top_down_role: Regimes where recession evidence does or does not certify unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Recession-Slope with Unbounded Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex example showing that a negative recession slope is sufficient but not necessary for an objective value of minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[1,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=-\log x\). Then \(C^\infty=\mathbb R_+\), and for every \(d>0\), \[f^\infty(d)=0.\] Nevertheless, \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\). Hence failure to find a direction with strictly negative recession value does not certify boundedness below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex problem can be unbounded below even though every feasible recession direction has zero, rather than negative, recession value.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=-\log x\) on \(C\), extended by positive infinity outside \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_C f=-\infty\) while no \(d\in C^\infty\) satisfies \(f^\infty(d)<0\).

notation.meaning: Recession function of the extended objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Recession-Slope with Finite Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp example showing that zero recession value does not certify unbounded descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(f\equiv0\). Every \(d\in C^\infty\) satisfies \(f^\infty(d)=0\), yet \(\inf_C f=0\). Thus replacing \(f^\infty(d)<0\) by \(f^\infty(d)\leq0\) is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant objective has zero recession value in every direction but a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonzero direction has zero recession value, but the problem is not unbounded below.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), a nonzero \(d\in C^\infty\) with \(f^\infty(d)<0\) certifies \(x_0+td\in C\) and \(f(x_0+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). If merely \(f^\infty(d)=0\), the ray certifies nonincrease but not divergence to \(-\infty\). A vector outside \(C^\infty\), or one lacking a feasible base point, is not an unboundedness certificate. Conversely, failure to exhibit such a direction does not by itself certify a finite attained optimum; infeasibility, nonattainment, and nonclosed representations remain possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-cost recession direction based at a finite feasible point certifies unboundedness; zero recession cost, an infeasible base, or failure to find a direction does not.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Two-by-Two Semidefinite Weakly Infeasible System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal semidefinite example of zero-distance infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[X(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\] the system \(X(t)\succeq0\) is infeasible for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname{dist}(X(t),\mathbb S_+^2)\to0\) as \(t\to+\infty\). Thus this affine semidefinite system is weakly infeasible and admits no positive-margin separating certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matrices [[t,1],[1,0]] are never positive semidefinite, but their distance to the semidefinite cone tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^2\) is the cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite \(2\times2\) matrices.
Distance is measured in any norm on the finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb S^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X(t)\notin\mathbb S_+^2\) for every \(t\), while \(\operatorname{dist}(X(t),\mathbb S_+^2)\to0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and Approximate-Feasibility Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional weak infeasibility for an equality-form conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. The system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is weakly infeasible exactly when \[b\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K).\] Equivalently, it is infeasible and there exists a sequence \(x_k\in K\) such that \(Ax_k\to b\). Every such approximate-feasibility sequence is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak conic infeasibility means that the right-hand side lies in the closure but not the image of the cone; approximate feasible points exist and necessarily escape to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is weakly infeasible iff \(b\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\), equivalently iff it is infeasible but admits \(x_k\in K\) with \(Ax_k\to b\); every such sequence is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure and Approximate-Feasibility Characterization

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq Y\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak infeasibility lies at zero distance from feasibility and therefore admits no strict separating certificate of the usual alternative type.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility boundary between strong and weak infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic system \(Ax-b\in K\) is weakly infeasible when \(S\cap K=\varnothing\) but \(\operatorname{dist}(S,K)=0\). In this case no \(y\in K^*\) can satisfy simultaneously \(A^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle>0\), because such a strict separator would imply a positive distance between \(S\) and \(K\). Thus standard finite strict-separation certificates cover strong infeasibility, where \(\operatorname{dist}(S,K)>0\), but not weak infeasibility; closure-sensitive or asymptotic certificates are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is weakly infeasible when it is infeasible yet has zero distance from feasibility, preventing an ordinary strict-separation certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-Infeasibility Boundary for Conic Feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E,F\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and consider \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\). Set \(C=A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility where the linear image of the cone may fail to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic system is weakly infeasible when \[b\notin C\qquad\text{and}\qquad b\in\operatorname{cl}C.\] Equivalently, \[\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\qquad\text{and}\qquad \inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0.\] It is strongly infeasible when \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}C\), equivalently when the distance from \(b\) to \(C\) is positive. The boundary of ordinary strict-separation certificates is therefore \[\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K).\] At a weakly infeasible datum, there is no vector \(y\) satisfying \[A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle y,b\rangle<0,\] because every such inequality would strictly separate \(b\) from \(\operatorname{cl}A(K)\). Instead, weak infeasibility is witnessed only asymptotically by sequences \(x_k\in K\) with \(Ax_k\to b\), unless a stronger problem-specific facial-reduction certificate is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is weakly infeasible when it has no feasible point but its residual infimum is zero. Geometrically, the right-hand side lies in the closure of the conic image but not in the image itself. This is exactly the boundary where strict Farkas separators cease to exist. Strong infeasibility places the right-hand side outside the closure and at positive distance from the image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak infeasibility is \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), equivalently infeasibility together with \(\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong infeasibility is characterized by \(\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K))>0\).
Weak infeasibility requires a sequence \(x_k\in K\) satisfying \(Ax_k\to b\) while no exact feasible point exists.
special_cases_latex: For polyhedral cones, linear images are closed, so weak infeasibility cannot occur in this form.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict conic Farkas certificate cannot exist at a weakly infeasible instance.
Numerical residuals can converge to zero even though the feasibility set is empty.
boundary_notes: An asymptotic sequence is not a finite exact certificate unless additional structure compresses it into one.
The definition concerns failure of closedness of the conic image, not merely ill-conditioning of a feasible system.

notation.meaning: Infimum of the norm distance from b to C.

review_flags: No supplied authoritative-source hint was located that explicitly defines weak conic infeasibility as closure-minus-image and states the strict-certificate boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbational value-sensitivity geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) be the decision space, \(U=\mathbb{R}^r\) the perturbation space, and \(F:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) an extended-real perturbation function. The nominal objective is \(f(x)=F(x,0)\), and the associated value function is \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation geometry of optimal values and dual supporting covectors; stability of the full solution mapping is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The perturbational value-sensitivity geometry of \(F\) at a parameter \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}p\) is the collection consisting of the marginal value \(p\), its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}p\), and its supporting covectors
\[
\partial p(\bar u)=\{s\in U: p(u)\ge p(\bar u)+\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle\ \text{for every }u\in U\}.
\]
A vector \(s\in\partial p(\bar u)\) is a first-order value-sensitivity covector: it supplies the global affine estimate
\[
p(u)-p(\bar u)\ge \langle s,u-\bar u\rangle\qquad(u\in U).
\]
For the nominal parameter, the geometry is based at \(\bar u=0\), where \(p(0)=\inf_x f(x)\). With the sign convention
\[
q(\mu)=\inf_{u\in U}\{p(u)+\langle\mu,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-\mu),
\]
a dual optimizer \(\mu\) corresponds, when strong duality and dual attainment hold, to the supporting covector \(-\mu\in\partial p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation function assigns an optimization problem to each parameter. Its value function records the corresponding infimum. At a parameter in the effective domain, the value-sensitivity geometry consists of the value-function epigraph and all covectors defining supporting affine lower bounds there. Under the stated dual sign convention, attained dual multipliers are the negatives of these supporting covectors.
assumptions_latex: \(p(\bar u)\in\mathbb{R}\) whenever the local sensitivity set \(\partial p(\bar u)\) is discussed.
For the multiplier interpretation, \(p\) is proper convex, the nominal primal and dual values are finite and equal, and the dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{G}_p(\bar u):=(\operatorname{epi}p,\partial p(\bar u)),\qquad p(u)\ge p(\bar u)+\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle\quad(s\in\partial p(\bar u)).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper convex \(p\), \(s\in\partial p(\bar u)\) is equivalent to \(p(\bar u)+p^*(s)=\langle s,\bar u\rangle\).
At \(\bar u=0\), \(-\mu\in\partial p(0)\) is equivalent to \(p(u)\ge p(0)-\langle\mu,u\rangle\) for all \(u\).
special_cases_latex: If \(p\) is differentiable at \(\bar u\), then \(\partial p(\bar u)=\{\nabla p(\bar u)\}\).
For right-hand-side constraint perturbations, the components of \(-\mu\) are marginal changes of the optimal value with respect to the corresponding perturbation coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonemptiness of \(\partial p(\bar u)\) gives a finite global first-order lower estimate for every admissible perturbation.
The relation \(q(\mu)=-p^*(-\mu)\) identifies dual optimization with the search for supporting hyperplanes of \(\operatorname{epi}p\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert differentiability, local Lipschitz continuity, primal attainment, or stability of minimizers.
At boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}p\), directional behavior may be infinite even when a subgradient exists.

notation.meaning: The Fenchel conjugate of the value function.
The convex subdifferential of the value function at the base parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric perturbation model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(U=\mathbb{R}^r\), and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be the nominal objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-real perturbation models for finite-dimensional minimization; particular objective, constraint, operator, and set perturbations arise by choosing a specific function \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A perturbation model for the nominal problem \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is an extended-real function
\[
F:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}
\]
satisfying
\[
F(x,0)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.
\]
For each \(u\in U\), the perturbed problem, its value, and its solution set are
\[
(P_u):\ \inf_{x\in X}F(x,u),\qquad p(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u),\qquad S(u):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x,u).
\]
The effective perturbation domain is
\[
\operatorname{dom}p:=\{u\in U:p(u)<+\infty\}.
\]
Thus \(p(u)=+\infty\) represents infeasibility in models encoded by indicator functions, while \(p(u)=-\infty\) represents an unbounded-below perturbed problem. The associated perturbational dual function under the adopted sign convention is
\[
q(\mu):=\inf_{(x,u)\in X\times U}\bigl(F(x,u)+\langle\mu,u\rangle\bigr)
       =\inf_{u\in U}\bigl(p(u)+\langle\mu,u\rangle\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation model embeds the nominal objective into a family indexed by a parameter whose zero value recovers the original problem. Partial minimization over the decision variable defines the value function, while exact minimizers define the solution mapping. Extended-real values distinguish infeasibility from unboundedness. Minimizing the perturbed value plus a linear parameter term produces the associated dual function.
assumptions_latex: \(0\in U\) is the distinguished nominal parameter.
The equality \(F(\cdot,0)=f\) holds pointwise, including extended-real values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(x,0)=f(x),\qquad p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u),\qquad S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,u),\qquad q(\mu)=\inf_u\{p(u)+\langle\mu,u\rangle\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph of the value function satisfies \(\operatorname{epi}p=\{(u,\alpha):\inf_xF(x,u)\leq\alpha\}\).
Using conjugacy, \(q(\mu)=-p^*(-\mu)=-F^*(0,-\mu)\) whenever the displayed conjugates are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
special_cases_latex: A constraint model is obtained from \(F(x,u)=f(x)+\delta_{C(u)}(x)\).
An additive objective model is obtained from \(F(x,u)=f(x)+\psi(x,u)\) with \(\psi(x,0)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The nominal value and solution set are \(p(0)=\inf_xf(x)\) and \(S(0)=\operatorname*{argmin}_xf(x)\).
If \(F\) is jointly convex, then its marginal value function \(p\) is convex, subject to the usual exclusion of the identically \(-\infty\) degeneracy.
boundary_notes: The definition permits empty solution sets even when the value is finite.
Convexity, closedness, and attainment are additional properties, not parts of the basic perturbation-model definition.

notation.meaning: The extended-real indicator of a set.
The exact solution set of the perturbed problem.

Scalar inequality and affine-equality right-hand-side perturbations arise from product cones containing \(\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linearly perturbed objective value is
\[p(c)=\inf_{x\in C}\bigl(f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle\bigr)=-\bigl(f+\iota_C\bigr)^*(-c),\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Consequently \(p\) is concave wherever finite. If \(x_c\) attains the infimum, then for every \(d\in X\), \(p(d)\le p(c)+\langle d-c,x_c\rangle\), so \(x_c\) is a supergradient of \(p\) at \(c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Minimizer–Supergradient Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact converse to the accepted seed's minimizer-to-supergradient inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:=f+\iota_C\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(p(c)=\inf_x\{h(x)+\langle c,x\rangle\}\). Whenever \(p(c)\) is finite, \(\partial^+p(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{h(x)+\langle c,x\rangle\}\). At an interior point of \(\operatorname{dom}p\), \(p\) is differentiable exactly when the perturbed minimizer is unique, and then \(\nabla p(c)\) equals that minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supergradients of the tilted value are exactly the tilted minimizers; uniqueness corresponds to differentiability at interior points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^+p(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{h(x)+\langle c,x\rangle\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h=f+\iota_C\) is proper, closed, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\), then every tilted problem has a unique minimizer \(x(c)\), the value \(p(c)=\inf_x(h(x)+\langle c,x\rangle)\) is differentiable, and \(\nabla p(c)=x(c)\) with \(\|x(c)-x(d)\|\leq\mu^{-1}\|c-d\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity makes the tilted minimizer unique and Lipschitz in the objective perturbation, with the minimizer equal to the value gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive and linear-tilt objective perturbations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(U=\mathbb{R}^r\), and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be the nominal objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-only perturbations: the admissible decision set is unchanged and the parameter modifies the objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An additive objective perturbation of \(f\) is specified by a function \(\psi:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) satisfying \(\psi(x,0)=0\) on \(\operatorname{dom}f\), through
\[
F(x,u):=f(x)+\psi(x,u),\qquad p(u):=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\psi(x,u)\}.
\]
The canonical linear-tilt model takes a linear map \(B:X\to U\) and sets
\[
F(x,u)=f(x)-\langle u,Bx\rangle,
\qquad
p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)-\langle u,Bx\rangle\}=-f^*(B^*u).
\]
Its exact minimizers are
\[
S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{f(x)-\langle u,Bx\rangle\}.
\]
For proper closed convex \(f\), a point \(x\) belongs to \(S(u)\) exactly when
\[
B^*u\in\partial f(x),
\]
or, equivalently, when \(x\in\partial f^*(B^*u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective perturbation keeps the decision domain fixed and adds a parameter-dependent term that vanishes at the nominal parameter. The standard linear tilt subtracts the pairing of the parameter with a linear observation of the decision. Its value is the negative conjugate of the nominal objective evaluated at the adjoint-transformed parameter. For a closed proper convex objective, minimizers are characterized by the corresponding subgradient relation.
assumptions_latex: For the conjugate and subgradient characterizations, \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(B\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(u)=\inf_x\{f(x)-\langle u,Bx\rangle\}=-f^*(B^*u),\qquad S(u)=\{x:B^*u\in\partial f(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in S(u)\) if and only if \(f(x)+f^*(B^*u)=\langle B^*u,x\rangle\).
When \(B\) is the identity, \(p(u)=-f^*(u)\) and \(S(u)=\partial f^*(u)\).
special_cases_latex: A scalar cost perturbation has \(\psi(x,u)=u\,h(x)\).
A linear coefficient perturbation of \(c^Tx\) is obtained by replacing \(c\) with \(c-B^*u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The tilt value \(p\) is concave in \(u\), being the negative of a convex conjugate composed with a linear map.
If \(f^*\) is differentiable at \(B^*u\), then all tilted minimizers have the same image determined by \(\nabla f^*(B^*u)\).
boundary_notes: This record does not cover perturbations that change feasibility.
The value may equal \(-\infty\) when the tilt destroys boundedness below.

notation.meaning: The adjoint of the linear map defining the tilt.
The Fenchel conjugate of the nominal objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled operator-and-data perturbation model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), \(U\) be a finite-dimensional parameter space, \(K\subseteq Y\) a fixed closed convex cone, and \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal finite-dimensional model in which the same parameter changes a linear operator and its right-hand-side data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An operator-data perturbation coupling is a pair of parameterized maps
\[
A:U\to\mathcal{L}(X,Y),\qquad b:U\to Y,
\]
with nominal data \(A(0)=A_0\) and \(b(0)=b_0\). It generates the feasible-set mapping and value function
\[
C(u):=\{x\in X:A(u)x-b(u)\in-K\},
\qquad
p(u):=\inf_{x\in C(u)}f(x).
\]
Equivalently, the extended-real perturbation function is
\[
F(x,u):=f(x)+\delta_{-K}(A(u)x-b(u)),
\qquad p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u).
\]
For affine parameterizations
\[
A(u)=A_0+\sum_{j=1}^r u_jA_j,
\qquad
b(u)=b_0+\sum_{j=1}^r u_jb_j,
\]
the parameter affects feasibility through the coupled residual
\[
R(x,u)=A_0x-b_0+\sum_{j=1}^ru_j(A_jx-b_j).
\]
The term “coupled” records that operator and datum are not treated as independent perturbation coordinates unless the parameter space is explicitly split.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator-data coupling assigns both a linear operator and right-hand-side data to each perturbation parameter. Feasibility is defined by membership of their residual in the negative cone, and the value is the infimum of the fixed objective over that feasible set. An extended-real indicator gives an equivalent unconstrained representation. In the affine model, each parameter coordinate changes the residual through both an operator action and a data shift.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a fixed closed convex cone.
The objective \(f\) is not itself perturbed in this model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(x,u)=f(x)+\delta_{-K}(A(u)x-b(u)),\qquad p(u)=\inf\{f(x):A(u)x-b(u)\in-K\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The feasibility condition is \(b(u)-A(u)x\in K\).
Equality constraints arise by taking \(K=\{0\}\), giving \(A(u)x=b(u)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A(u)\equiv A_0\), the model reduces to a right-hand-side data perturbation.
If \(b(u)\equiv b_0\), it reduces to an operator-only perturbation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective parameter domain is \(\{u:C(u)\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\}\) unless the infimum is \(-\infty\).
Even when \(f\) and \(K\) are convex, joint convexity in \((x,u)\) can fail because \(A(u)x\) is bilinear.
boundary_notes: No continuity or differentiability of \(A(\cdot)\) or \(b(\cdot)\) is built into the definition.
A precise authoritative locator supporting this exact coupled formulation was not identified among the supplied source hints.

notation.meaning: The space of linear maps from the decision space to the residual space.
The extended-real indicator of the negative cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint Transmission of an Operator Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of constraint-operator variation on the Lagrangian stationarity term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((A+E)x-b\in-K\) and \(y\in K^*\),
\[L_E(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,(A+E)x-b\rangle=f(x)+\langle A^*y+E^*y,x\rangle-\langle y,b\rangle.\]
Hence \(A\mapsto A+E\) changes the adjoint stationarity coefficient by exactly \(E^*y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal operator perturbation is transmitted to Lagrangian stationarity through the adjoint term E-star applied to the multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone, and \(f\) is proper convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual-side coefficient changes from \(A^*y\) to \(A^*y+E^*y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Transmission of an Operator Perturbation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Decision Boundary for Uniform Operator Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform displacement induced by a small operator perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(S\subseteq X\) satisfies \(\sup_{x\in S}\|x\|\leq R<\infty\), then
\[\sup_{x\in S}\|Ex\|\leq R\|E\|.\]
Conversely, if \(S\) contains a ray \(\{x_0+th:t\geq0\}\), then every \(E\) with \(Eh\neq0\) satisfies \(\sup_{x\in S}\|Ex\|=+\infty\). Thus no finite constant \(c\) can make \(\sup_{x\in S}\|Ex\|\leq c\|E\|\) valid for a perturbation class containing such an \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator perturbations are uniformly controlled on bounded decision sets, while an affected feasible ray destroys any finite uniform bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and \(E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\).
For the failure statement, \(S\) contains a ray of direction \(h\) and \(Eh\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded decision magnitude suffices for uniform control, while an affected ray precludes it.

notation.meaning: Decision set on which displacement is measured

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Decision Boundary for Uniform Operator Control

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex, and \(b\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An operator perturbation changes the constraint image through the bilinear term \(Ex\), not through a fixed right-hand-side translation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear conic constraints with perturbation in the constraint operator alone.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), the operator-perturbed conic program has value
\[v(E)=\inf\{f(x):(A+E)x-b\in-K\},\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), and nominal value \(v(0)\). Unlike an additive constraint perturbation, \(E\) contributes \(Ex\), which depends on the decision variable. Sensitivity is therefore measured in a specified operator norm on \(\mathcal L(X,Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator perturbation replaces the constraint map by a nearby linear map, creating a decision-dependent displacement measured in an operator norm.

children.title: Problem-Data Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations applied to coefficients, right-hand sides, or other problem data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Data Perturbations in the Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transmission of objective and right-hand-side data into the conic Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y\in K^*\),
\[L_{c,d}(x,y)=f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle+\langle y,Ax-b-d\rangle=f(x)+\langle c+A^*y,x\rangle-\langle y,b+d\rangle.\]
Thus \(c\) shifts the stationarity coefficient and \(d\) shifts the multiplier payoff by \(-\langle y,d\rangle\). For every feasible \(x\), \(L_{c,d}(x,y)\leq f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective data enter stationarity, right-hand-side data enter the multiplier payoff, and dual-cone multipliers yield weak-duality lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: The assumptions of the data-perturbed conic model hold.
\(y\in K^*\) under the nonnegative dual-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two data components have distinct Lagrangian roles, and every dual-cone multiplier provides a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Data Perturbations in the Lagrangian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sectional Curvature of the Data Value Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature in objective-coefficient and right-hand-side sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[v(c,d)=\inf\{f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle:Ax-(b+d)\in-K\},\]
the map \(c\mapsto v(c,d)\) is concave for fixed \(d\), and \(d\mapsto v(c,d)\) is convex for fixed \(c\). Joint convexity or concavity need not hold. For example, minimizing \(\tfrac12x^2+cx\) subject to \(x\geq d\) gives, on the region \(d>-c\),
\[v(c,d)=\tfrac12d^2+cd,\]
whose Hessian is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value is concave in the objective tilt and convex in the right-hand-side displacement separately, but generally has neither curvature jointly.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data value map has opposite sectional curvature, while the joint map can be neither convex nor concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Sectional Curvature of the Data Value Map

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Problem-data perturbations translate the objective and constraint data while retaining the nominal operator and cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear objective and right-hand-side data perturbations with operator and cone fixed.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nominal right-hand side \(b\in Y\), define the data-perturbed value
\[v(c,d)=\inf\{f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle:Ax-(b+d)\in-K\},\]
where \((c,d)\in X\times Y\) and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The nominal problem is \((c,d)=(0,0)\). This model perturbs the linear objective coefficient and right-hand side while keeping \(A\), \(f\), and \(K\) fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Problem-data perturbations tilt the objective and shift the right-hand side while preserving the constraint operator and ordering cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Data Perturbations

children.title: Coupled Operator–Data Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes where operator and data changes interact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Residual Coupling and Uniform-Control Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual geometry when the constraint operator, right-hand side, and decision vary simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r(x;E,d)=(A+E)x-(b+d)\). For a decision displacement \(h\),
\[r(x+h;E,d)-r(x;0,0)=Ah+Ex-d+Eh.\]
Thus simultaneous operator and decision changes produce the bilinear term \(Eh\). Also,
\[\|Ex-d\|\leq \|E\|\,\|x\|+\|d\|.\]
Consequently, \((E,d)\to(0,0)\) gives uniform residual control on bounded decision sets, whereas operator-norm smallness alone gives no uniform control on a set containing a ray affected nontrivially by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint operator and data perturbations contain an operator–decision cross term; uniform residual control requires bounded decisions or an equivalent size bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A,E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), \(b,d\in Y\), and \(\|E\|\) is the subordinate operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact residual expansion contains \(Eh\), and uniform control by perturbation norms requires control of decision magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Residual Coupling and Uniform-Control Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint value map captures interaction between operator and additive data changes through \((A+E)x-(b+d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint finite-dimensional perturbation of a linear conic operator and its objective/right-hand-side data.

source_refs.locator: 6 Convex Cones and Generalized Interiors p. 111
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), \(c\in X\), and \(d\in Y\), define
\[V(E,c,d)=\inf\{f(x)+\langle c,x\rangle:(A+E)x-(b+d)\in-K\},\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The nominal value is \(V(0,0,0)\). Because the constraint displacement equals \(Ex-d\), operator and data effects generally cannot be represented by one decision-independent translation uniformly over \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint perturbations change the operator, objective coefficient, and right-hand side; the operator and data effects interact through the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Operator–Data Perturbations

The cited cone section does not inspectably support coupled operator, objective, and right-hand-side perturbations or the stated nonrepresentability by a uniform translation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Coupling and the Bilinear Remainder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual geometry when both the constraint operator and right-hand-side data vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r(x;E,d)=(A+E)x-(b+d)\). For a decision displacement \(h\),
\[r(x+h;E,d)-r(x;0,0)=Ah+Ex-d+Eh.\]
Thus the operator and decision perturbations have the bilinear remainder \(Eh\). Moreover,
\[\|Ex-d\|\leq \|E\|\,\|x\|+\|d\|.\]
Consequently, small \((E,d)\) gives a uniform small residual displacement on bounded decision sets, but operator-norm smallness alone gives no uniform bound over an unbounded decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous operator and data perturbations have a bilinear operator–decision interaction. Uniform residual control requires bounded decisions or another bound on their size.
assumptions_latex: \(A,E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), \(b,d\in Y\), and the operator norm is subordinate to the chosen norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact residual expansion contains the coupling term \(Eh\), and uniform control by \(\|E\|\) requires control of decision magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Coupling and the Bilinear Remainder

children.title: Representation-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of perturbation behavior on the selected representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nominal Equivalence Does Not Preserve Calmness Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit boundary between nominal equivalence and equivalence of perturbation geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[P_1(u):\ \min_x |x|\ \text{ subject to }x=u,\qquad P_2(w):\ \min_x |x|\ \text{ subject to }x=w^2.\]
At parameter zero the problems have the same objective, feasible set \(\{0\}\), optimizer, and value. Their value functions are \(v_1(u)=|u|\) and \(v_2(w)=w^2\). Their exact calmness moduli at zero, defined by the corresponding local limsup ratios, are respectively \(1\) and \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two parameterizations can define the same nominal problem yet have different exact local sensitivity moduli.
assumptions_latex: Parameters and decisions are real scalars with the absolute-value norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nominal feasible-set and objective equivalence does not determine perturbational calmness.

notation.meaning: Two parameterized representations of the same nominal problem

knowledge_statements.title: Nominal Equivalence Does Not Preserve Calmness Moduli

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calmness Transfer Under Bi-Lipschitz Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for transferring local value sensitivity between representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1,v_2\) be finite-valued near their reference parameters. Suppose neighborhoods of \(0\) are related by a bijection \(\phi\) satisfying
\[\phi(0)=0,\quad v_2(\phi(u))=v_1(u),\quad \|\phi(u)\|\leq L\|u\|,\quad \|\phi^{-1}(w)\|\leq M\|w\|.\]
If \(|v_1(u)-v_1(0)|\leq\kappa_1\|u\|\) locally, then \(|v_2(w)-v_2(0)|\leq M\kappa_1\|w\|\) locally. Conversely, a calmness bound \(\kappa_2\) for \(v_2\) yields the bound \(L\kappa_2\) for \(v_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-preserving local bi-Lipschitz coordinate change transfers calmness in both directions, with constants scaled by coordinate distortion.
assumptions_latex: The value functions are finite-valued near zero.
The displayed value-preserving bijection and local forward and inverse Lipschitz bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local calmness transfers bidirectionally with multiplicative factors \(M\) and \(L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Transfer Under Bi-Lipschitz Reparameterization

assumptions_latex: Two formulations have the same nominal feasible set and objective values.
Perturbation size is measured in the native data norm of each formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nominal equivalence alone does not imply equality or comparable regularity of the associated value functions.

notation.meaning: Value functions induced by two representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating nominal problem equivalence from perturbational equivalence.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nominal equivalence gives only \(v_1(0)=v_2(0)\) and equality of nominal solution sets. It does not imply \(v_1(u)=v_2(u)\) near \(0\), nor equality of calmness moduli, condition numbers, or distances to infeasibility. Such sensitivity quantities are invariant only when the two perturbation parameterizations are locally related by norm-controlled maps that preserve corresponding perturbed feasible points and objective values in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent nominal formulations can have different sensitivity and conditioning unless their perturbation parameters correspond locally through norm-controlled, feasibility-preserving maps.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitivity Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

In addition, the assertion that invariance holds only under locally norm-controlled bidirectional maps is a broad necessity claim whose exact hypotheses and sensitivity notions require a dedicated variational-analysis or condition-number source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sensitivity Transfer Under Bi-Lipschitz Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for transferring local value-function regularity between equivalent perturbation representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1:U_1\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(v_2:U_2\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and suppose neighborhoods of \(0\) are related by a bijection \(\phi\) with \(\phi(0)=0\),
\[v_2(\phi(u))=v_1(u),\qquad \|\phi(u)\|\leq L\|u\|,\qquad \|\phi^{-1}(w)\|\leq M\|w\|.\]
Then calmness of \(v_1\) at \(0\) with modulus \(\kappa_1\) implies calmness of \(v_2\) with modulus at most \(M\kappa_1\), and calmness of \(v_2\) with modulus \(\kappa_2\) implies calmness of \(v_1\) with modulus at most \(L\kappa_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-preserving local bi-Lipschitz change of perturbation coordinates transfers calmness in both directions, with constants scaled by the coordinate distortion.
assumptions_latex: The displayed value-preserving bijection and local Lipschitz bounds hold.
All calmness statements use the displayed native parameter norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local calmness is invariant up to the multiplicative distortions \(L\) and \(M\).

notation.meaning: Forward and inverse local Lipschitz bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Sensitivity Transfer Under Bi-Lipschitz Reparameterization

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled feasible-set and ordering-cone perturbation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), \(U\) be a parameter space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and \(G:X\times U\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued perturbations in which both an admissible decision set and a constraint cone depend on the same parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-cone perturbation coupling consists of mappings
\[
C:U\rightrightarrows X,
\qquad
K:U\rightrightarrows Y,
\]
such that each \(K(u)\) is a cone, together with nominal objects \(C(0)=C_0\) and \(K(0)=K_0\). The perturbed feasible set and optimal value are
\[
\mathcal{F}(u):=\{x\in C(u):G(x,u)\in-K(u)\},
\qquad
p(u):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal{F}(u)}f(x).
\]
The equivalent extended-real representation is
\[
F(x,u)=f(x)+\delta_{C(u)}(x)+\delta_{-K(u)}(G(x,u)),
\qquad p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u).
\]
The coupling is genuine when the parameter cannot be decomposed as \(u=(u_C,u_K)\) so that \(C\) depends only on \(u_C\) and \(K\) only on \(u_K\). The polar multiplier cone at parameter \(u\) is
\[
K(u)^*:=\{y\in Y:\langle y,k\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }k\in K(u)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-cone perturbation uses one parameter to vary both the admissible decision set and the cone that orders the constraint residual. Feasible decisions belong to the varying set and have residual in the negative varying cone. Indicator functions combine these requirements into one extended-real objective. The dual multiplier domain changes with the polar of the perturbed cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K(u)\subseteq Y\) is a cone for every \(u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl[f(x)+\delta_{C(u)}(x)+\delta_{-K(u)}(G(x,u))\bigr].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal F(u)\) if and only if \(x\in C(u)\) and \(-G(x,u)\in K(u)\).
When \(K(u)\) is closed and convex, the compatible multiplier domain is its polar cone \(K(u)^*\).
special_cases_latex: Fixed-cone set perturbation: \(K(u)\equiv K_0\).
Fixed-set cone perturbation: \(C(u)\equiv C_0\).
Ordinary scalar inequalities arise from \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(K(u)=\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\mathcal F(u)=\varnothing\), then \(p(u)=+\infty\).
Variation of \(K(u)\) changes both primal feasibility and the admissible dual multiplier cone.
boundary_notes: Closedness, convexity, and graphical continuity of the set-valued maps are not part of the bare definition.
No inspected source among the supplied hints directly supported this exact simultaneous set-and-cone formulation.

notation.meaning: The positive polar cone under the stated sign convention.

review_flags: An authoritative source for the exact coupled set-cone definition is required.
Polar-cone sign conventions should be checked against the eventual chapter-wide convention.

children.title: Feasible-Set Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations applied directly to admissible sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(U\) is a parameter set containing \(0\).
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and each \(C_u\subseteq X\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible-set perturbation is represented by the extended-real objectives \(f+\iota_{C_u}\) and their infima.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued perturbations of feasibility with a fixed convex objective.

source_refs.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(u\in U\), let \(C_u\) be the perturbed feasible set, with nominal set \(C_0\). Define
\[v(u)=\inf_{x\in C_u}f(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\iota_{C_u}(x)\bigr),\]
where \(\iota_{C_u}(x)=0\) for \(x\in C_u\), \(\iota_{C_u}(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Because \(f\) and every \(C_u\) are convex, each extended-real objective \(f+\iota_{C_u}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-set perturbation replaces the nominal constraint set by a parameterized family; equivalently, it adds each set's indicator to a fixed convex objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Perturbations
