knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let \(L\) be a proper closed saddle function in Rockafellar's closed-saddle equivalence-class convention. Then \[T_L(x,y)=\{(u,-v):u\in\partial_xL(x,y),\ v\in\partial_y^+L(x,y)\}\] is maximal monotone on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed saddle subdifferential of a proper closed saddle function is maximal monotone.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a proper closed saddle function in Rockafellar's convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_L\text{ is maximal monotone on }X\times Y.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued saddle operator with a superdifferential in the concave variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
T(x,y)=\bigl\{(u,-v):u\in\partial_xL(x,y),\ v\in\partial_yL(x,y)\bigr\},
\]
where \(\partial_yL(x,y)\) denotes the concave superdifferential of \(L(x,\cdot)\). Then \(T\) is monotone: whenever \((u_i,w_i)\in T(x_i,y_i)\) for \(i=1,2\),
\[
\langle u_1-u_2,x_1-x_2\rangle+
\langle w_1-w_2,y_1-y_2\rangle\ge0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
(0,0)\in T(x^*,y^*)
\]
is equivalent to \(L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex-concave saddle function induces a monotone signed partial-subdifferential operator whose zeros are exactly its saddle points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone operator induced by a saddle function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous convex in \(x\), and upper-semicontinuous concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set-valued operator formulation for possibly nonsmooth convex–concave saddle functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monotone saddle operator associated with \(L\) is \(T_L(x,y):=(\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x))\times(\partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y))\). It is monotone when, for all \(u_i\in T_L(x_i,y_i)\), \(\langle u_1-u_2,(x_1-x_2,y_1-y_2)\rangle\geq0\). Its zero set is exactly the saddle set: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \((0,0)\in T_L(x^*,y^*)\). In the smooth case, the single-valued interior part is \((\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone saddle operator combines the subgradient in the minimizing variable with the negative subgradient in the maximizing variable and adds the two constraint normal cones. Solving the saddle problem is equivalent to finding a zero of this operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_L(x,y):=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x)\\ \partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad \operatorname{zer}T_L=\mathcal S(L).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the smooth case, \(T_L(x,y)=(\nabla_xL(x,y)+N_X(x),-\nabla_yL(x,y)+N_Y(y))\).
The zero inclusion is the coupled primal–dual stationarity system.
special_cases_latex: When \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), only the sectional subdifferentials remain.
For a bilinear coupling plus separable convex terms, \(T_L\) has the standard skew-linear primal–dual block structure.
immediate_consequences_latex: The zero set of a maximal monotone saddle operator is closed and convex.
Strict monotonicity permits at most one zero.
boundary_notes: Maximal monotonicity may require closedness and regularity beyond bare monotonicity.
The sign in the dual component is essential; using \(\partial_yL\) would not encode maximization.

notation.meaning: Set of points mapped to a set containing zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality model of a smooth saddle problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Let \(L:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, convex in \(x\in X\), and concave in \(y\in Y\). Put \(C:=X\times Y\) and \(F(x,y):=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth convex–concave saddle problems represented as monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational-inequality saddle model is \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\): find \((x^*,y^*)\in C\) such that \(\langle F(x^*,y^*),(x-x^*,y-y^*)\rangle\geq0\) for every \((x,y)\in C\). Because \(L\) is convex–concave, this condition is equivalent to the saddle inequalities \(L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\). It is also equivalent to \((0,0)\in F(x^*,y^*)+N_C(x^*,y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex–concave saddle problem becomes a variational inequality on the product feasible set when the field is formed from the primal gradient and the negative dual gradient. Solutions of the variational inequality are exactly saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\rangle-\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\rangle\geq0\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y.\]
special_cases_latex: For unconstrained sets, the model reduces to \(\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*)=0\) and \(\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*)=0\).
A bilinear payoff produces an affine monotone field.
immediate_consequences_latex: The field \(F\) is monotone on \(C\).
If \(F\) is strictly monotone, the variational inequality has at most one solution.
boundary_notes: For nonsmooth \(L\), the appropriate model is a generalized variational inequality or monotone inclusion.
For nonconvex–nonconcave \(L\), the variational inequality expresses stationarity but not necessarily a global saddle point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle-gap failure regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Z\) be nonempty and \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\). Define \(v_-:=\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\), \(v_+:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\), and \(\Gamma:=v_+-v_-\) whenever both values are finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global value-gap diagnosis for real-valued minimax problems; attainment failure is recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strict saddle-gap failure occurs when \(\Gamma>0\), equivalently \(v_-<v_+\). A zero-gap but uncertified-saddle regime occurs when \(\Gamma=0\) but one or both outer extrema are not attained. For a candidate pair \((x,z)\), its primal–dual saddle residual is \(G(x,z):=\sup_{z'\in Z}\phi(x,z')-\inf_{x'\in X}\phi(x',z)\geq0\). It vanishes exactly at saddle points. Thus \(\Gamma\) diagnoses failure of value interchange, whereas \(G\) diagnoses whether a particular pair is a saddle certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global saddle gap is the min–max value minus the max–min value. A positive gap means minimax interchange fails. The pairwise gap compares a candidate's worst dual response with its best primal response and equals zero exactly for saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Gamma:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)-\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\geq0,\qquad G(x,z)\geq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G(x,z)=0\iff \sup_{z'\in Z}\phi(x,z')=\phi(x,z)=\inf_{x'\in X}\phi(x',z).\]
\[\Gamma>0\iff \sup_Z\inf_X\phi<\inf_X\sup_Z\phi.\]
special_cases_latex: For convex–concave closed problems, lack of lower semicontinuity of an associated perturbation value at the origin can produce \(\Gamma>0\).
When \(\Gamma=0\) but the dual supremum is not attained, every pair has positive residual even though the values agree.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any pair with \(G(x,z)=0\) certifies \(\Gamma=0\) and attainment on both sides.
A positive \(\Gamma\) rules out every saddle point.
boundary_notes: The finite-value restriction avoids undefined expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\).
The global gap and pairwise residual are different objects and should not be conflated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimum Pointwise Gap Equals the Minimax Value Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite lower and upper minimax values; the pointwise-gap infimum need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\underline v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\) and \(\overline v:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\), and assume both values are finite. Then \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v.\] Thus the pointwise gaps have infimum zero exactly when the minimax values agree, although no zero-gap pair need exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of the pointwise gap is the upper-minus-lower minimax value gap; equality of values does not ensure attainment of a zero gap.
assumptions_latex: The pointwise gaps entering the infimum are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x,y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic decomposition of the unrestricted saddle gap when all terms are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x):=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\) and \(d(y):=\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\). Whenever \(p(x)\), \(d(y)\), and \(L(x,y)\) are finite, \[G(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)=[p(x)-L(x,y)]+[L(x,y)-d(y)].\] Both residuals are nonnegative, so the gap vanishes exactly when both vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle gap splits into two nonnegative best-response residuals, both of which vanish exactly at zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x),d(y),L(x,y)\) are finite at the evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)=[p(x)-L(x,y)]+[L(x,y)-d(y)]\), with both summands nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Pointwise Gap Equals the Minimax Value Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite lower and upper minimax values; the infimum need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\underline v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\) and \(\overline v:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\), and assume both are finite. Then every pair satisfies \(G(x,y)\geq\overline v-\underline v\), and \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v.\] Hence the best attainable pointwise gap is zero exactly when the minimax values agree, although a zero-gap pair need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of the pointwise gap is the upper-minus-lower minimax value gap; equality of values does not ensure that this infimum is attained.
assumptions_latex: The pointwise gaps used in the infimum are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x,y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v\).
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Pointwise Gap Equals the Minimax Value Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gap as Two Saddle Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic decomposition of the unrestricted pointwise saddle gap when all terms are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x):=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\) and \(d(y):=\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\). Whenever these values and \(L(x,y)\) are finite, \[G(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)=\bigl[p(x)-L(x,y)\bigr]+\bigl[L(x,y)-d(y)\bigr].\] Both bracketed residuals are nonnegative. Consequently, a zero gap is equivalent to simultaneous vanishing of the primal-response and dual-response residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle gap splits into two nonnegative best-response residuals, both of which vanish exactly at zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x),d(y),L(x,y)\) are finite at the evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)=[p(x)-L(x,y)]+[L(x,y)-d(y)]\), with both summands nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap as Two Saddle Residuals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual gap certificate for separable Lovász-extension optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded specialization of a primal–dual gap function to Lovász-extension optimization over a base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(s\in B(F)\), define \[\operatorname{gap}(w,s)=f(w)-w^\top s+\sum_{j=1}^p\left[\psi_j(w_j)+\psi_j^*(-s_j)+w_js_j\right].\] This is the primal objective value minus the dual objective value. Moreover, \(f(w)-w^\top s\ge 0\), and the Fenchel–Young inequality gives \(\psi_j(w_j)+\psi_j^*(-s_j)+w_js_j\ge 0\) for every \(j\). Hence \(\operatorname{gap}(w,s)\ge0\), and it equals zero if and only if \(f(w)-w^\top s=0\) and \(\psi_j(w_j)+\psi_j^*(-s_j)+w_js_j=0\) for every \(j\). The gap provides a suboptimality certificate for both candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-minus-dual objective gap decomposes into a nonnegative Lovász support discrepancy and nonnegative coordinatewise Fenchel–Young discrepancies. It vanishes exactly when every discrepancy vanishes and certifies the suboptimality of both feasible candidates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the Lovász extension associated with \(F\)
\(\psi_j^*\) is the Fenchel conjugate of \(\psi_j\) for every \(j\)
The primal and dual objectives are those of the associated separable Lovász-extension dual pair
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}(w,s)\ge0\), and \(\operatorname{gap}(w,s)=0\) iff \(f(w)-w^\top s=0\) and \(\psi_j(w_j)+\psi_j^*(-s_j)+w_js_j=0\) for every \(j\); this gap is a primal and dual suboptimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gap restricted to \(X'\) and \(Y'\) is \[G_{X',Y'}(x,y):=\sup_{v\in Y'}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X'}L(u,y).\] Because \(x\in X'\) and \(y\in Y'\), one has \(G_{X',Y'}(x,y)\geq0\). When both optimized terms are finite, \(G_{X',Y'}(x,y)=0\) if and only if \[L(x,v)\leq L(x,y)\leq L(u,y)\qquad\text{for all }u\in X'\text{ and }v\in Y'.\] A zero restricted gap need not imply a global saddle point unless \(X'=X\) and \(Y'=Y\), or additional approximation guarantees are supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted gap tests saddle inequalities against selected comparison sets. For a point belonging to both comparison sets, a finite zero gap is exactly the restricted saddle condition, but it is not generally a global saddle certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity under Enlargement of Comparison Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order property of restricted gaps at a fixed evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X_1\subseteq X_2\subseteq X\), \(Y_1\subseteq Y_2\subseteq Y\), and \((x,y)\in X_1\times Y_1\), then, whenever the displayed gaps are defined, \[G_{X_1,Y_1}(x,y)\leq G_{X_2,Y_2}(x,y)\leq G_{X,Y}(x,y).\] Thus enlarging either comparison set strengthens the test, while a small restricted gap alone gives no upper bound on the unrestricted gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted gaps increase when either comparison set is enlarged and never exceed the unrestricted gap.
assumptions_latex: All displayed extended-real differences are defined.

notation.meaning: gap restricted to comparison sets A and B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery from Exhausting Comparison Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise monotone recovery of the unrestricted gap through nested comparison sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_k\uparrow X\) and \(Y_k\uparrow Y\), with \((x,y)\in X_1\times Y_1\). If all displayed differences are defined and the unrestricted gap does not have an indeterminate \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) or \((-\infty)-(-\infty)\) form, then \[G_{X_k,Y_k}(x,y)\uparrow G_{X,Y}(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along nested comparison sets exhausting the full domains, restricted gaps increase to the unrestricted gap whenever the extended-real subtraction is well defined.
assumptions_latex: Every displayed gap and its limit are defined in extended-real arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}G_{X_k,Y_k}(x,y)=G_{X,Y}(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery from Exhausting Comparison Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bilinear Noncompact Interchange Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued convex–concave payoff on noncompact open convex domains with an extended-real minimax gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=xy\). This payoff is affine in each variable. For every \(y>0\), \(\inf_{x>0}xy=0\), whereas for every \(x>0\), \(\sup_{y>0}xy=+\infty\). Hence \[\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}L(x,y)=0<+\infty=\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}L(x,y).\] Thus separate convexity–concavity alone does not justify minimax interchange on noncompact domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The payoff xy on two positive half-lines has lower minimax value zero and upper minimax value positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}xy=0<+\infty=\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}xy\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Noncompact Interchange Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Minimax Interchange Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-level failure under the minimization–maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), let \(\underline v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\) and \(\overline v:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\). Weak minimax gives \(\underline v\leq\overline v\). Minimax interchange fails at the value level exactly when \(\underline v<\overline v\), including a strict extended-real inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimax interchange fails when the lower minimax value is strictly smaller than the upper minimax value.
assumptions_latex: The displayed extended-real infima and suprema are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{minimax interchange failure}\iff \underline v<\overline v\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Minimax Interchange Failure

assumptions_latex: \(L(x,y)=x-y\), which is affine in each variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=0<+\infty=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact convex domains show that convexity-concavity alone does not justify minimax interchange.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=x-y\). The function is finite, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\), but the domains are noncompact. For each \(y>0\), \(\inf_{x>0}(x-y)=-y\), hence \[\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}L(x,y)=0.\] For every \(x>0\), \(\sup_{y>0}(x-y)=x\), not \(+\infty\). Therefore \[\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}L(x,y)=0.\] Thus this example does not produce interchange failure; an authoritative concrete counterexample remains required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The obvious affine noncompact example has equal minimax values, so it does not establish failure. A valid concrete convex-concave counterexample and supporting source are still required.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Interchange Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,1)\) and \(L(x,y)=x-y\). Then \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\sup_{0<y<1}(-y)=0\] and \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\inf_{0<x<1}x=0.\] Hence a finite saddle value exists. Nevertheless, no \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point: the primal infimum requires \(x=0\) and the dual supremum requires \(y=0\), neither of which belongs to its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On two open unit intervals, the affine payoff has equal finite minimax values, but the required extrema occur at excluded boundary points, so no saddle point exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Value without a Saddle Point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment Characterization at a Common Saddle Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equality of minimax values from simultaneous attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the finite common value \[v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\] exists. A saddle point exists if and only if there are \(x^\star\in X\) and \(y^\star\in Y\) such that \[\sup_{y\in Y}L(x^\star,y)=v=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^\star).\] In that case \(L(x^\star,y^\star)=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With equal finite minimax values, a saddle point exists exactly when both response-value extrema attain the common value.
assumptions_latex: The lower and upper minimax values are equal and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L)\neq\varnothing\iff\exists(x^\star,y^\star):\sup_yL(x^\star,y)=v=\inf_xL(x,y^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Characterization at a Common Saddle Value

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common saddle value without saddle attainment
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Z\) be nonempty, let \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\), and suppose the values \(v_-:=\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\) and \(v_+:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued minimax equality with failure of at least one outer attainment condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem has a saddle value without a saddle point when \(v_-=v_+=:v\in\mathbb R\) but the saddle set is empty. Equivalently, the common value exists while \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\) or \(Z^*:=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\) is empty. This regime separates minimax value equality from saddle attainment: \(v\) is well defined even though no pair realizes both inequalities of a saddle certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle value can exist even though no saddle point does. This happens when max–min equals min–max but at least one of the two outer optimization problems does not attain its optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v_-=v_+=v\in\mathbb R,\qquad \mathcal S(\phi)=\varnothing\iff X^*=\varnothing\text{ or }Z^*=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every \((x,z)\in X\times Z\) has strictly positive pairwise saddle residual \(G(x,z)\), although \(\inf_{x,z}G(x,z)\) may be zero.
There can exist optimizing sequences \(x_k\) and \(z_k\) whose marginal values converge to \(v\) without a convergent optimizer in the domain.
special_cases_latex: For \(X=\mathbb R\), \(Z=\mathbb R_+\), and \(\phi(x,z)=x+zx^2\), both minimax values equal \(0\), but the dual supremum is not attained.
Compactness of both strategy sets together with appropriate semicontinuity excludes this regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: A numerical value equality is not an existence certificate.
Any valid saddle certificate would force both outer optima to be attained, contradicting this regime.
boundary_notes: This is distinct from a positive minimax gap: here the two values are equal.
The definition requires a finite common value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment Characterization of a Saddle Point at a Common Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equality of minimax values from simultaneous attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the finite common value \[v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\] exists. A saddle point exists if and only if there are \(x^\star\in X\) and \(y^\star\in Y\) such that \[\sup_{y\in Y}L(x^\star,y)=v=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^\star).\] In that case \(L(x^\star,y^\star)=v\). Consequently, a saddle value exists without a saddle point exactly when the common value is finite but no pair of primal and dual response sections simultaneously attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With equal finite minimax values, a saddle point exists exactly when an upper-value minimizer and a lower-value maximizer both attain the common value.
assumptions_latex: The lower and upper minimax values are equal and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L)\neq\varnothing\iff\exists(x^\star,y^\star):\sup_yL(x^\star,y)=v=\inf_xL(x,y^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Characterization of a Saddle Point at a Common Value

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural duality failure-and-repair taxonomy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a primal–dual pair \((P),(D)\), write \(p^*:=\inf(P)\), \(d^*:=\sup(D)\), \(P^*,D^*\) for the optimizer sets, and \(\Delta:=p^*-d^*\) whenever the values are finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex and conic duality diagnostics; repairs are structural reformulations or qualification restorations, not numerical solution procedures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The failure status of a primal–dual pair is the signature \(\Sigma(P,D):=(\operatorname{feas}P,\operatorname{feas}D,\operatorname{att}P,\operatorname{att}D,\Delta,\operatorname{qual})\). Its canonical classes are infeasibility, unboundedness, positive gap \(\Delta>0\), zero-gap nonattainment, and certificate or qualification degeneracy. A structural repair is a transformation to an equivalent or explicitly relaxed pair whose signature removes the targeted failure while preserving the intended primal value or clearly recording any relaxation. Standard repair types include imposing a relative-interior qualification, restricting to the minimal cone face, closing a perturbation or image set, and homogenizing an infeasibility system to expose a separating certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy classifies a dual pair by feasibility, boundedness, attainment, gap, and qualification status. Repairs address the diagnosed structural defect—for example by restoring a relative-interior condition, reducing to the minimal face, closing a value representation, or exposing an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Sigma(P,D):=(\mathrm{feas}_P,\mathrm{feas}_D,\mathrm{att}_P,\mathrm{att}_D,\Delta,\mathrm{qual}),\qquad \Delta=p^*-d^*\geq0\text{ under weak duality}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A positive-gap failure has finite \(p^*,d^*\) with \(p^*>d^*\).
A zero-gap nonattainment failure has \(p^*=d^*\) but \(P^*=\varnothing\) or \(D^*=\varnothing\).
A qualification failure records absence of the regularity needed for the desired strong-duality or attainment implication, whether or not a gap actually occurs.
special_cases_latex: In conic programming, strict feasibility is a standard repair-enabling qualification.
Weak conic infeasibility motivates facial reduction or extended certificates because ordinary strict separation is unavailable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different failures can coexist, so the status is a signature rather than a single label.
A repair must state whether it preserves the original feasible set, only the value, or merely a relaxation bound.
boundary_notes: The cited sources support the constituent gap, attainment, strict-feasibility, and conic-status distinctions; the tuple notation is a local organizational definition.
Solver algorithms and convergence claims are outside this taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric solvability statuses of a conic system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Write \(L:=\{Ax-b:x\in\mathbb R^n\}\) and \(F:=L\cap K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine conic feasibility systems \(Ax-b\in K\), classified by intersection and distance geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic feasibility status is determined by the position of the affine space \(L\) relative to \(K\): strictly feasible if \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\); boundary-feasible if \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\) but \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\); strongly infeasible if \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0\); and weakly infeasible if \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\). These four regimes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is strictly feasible when its affine image enters the cone interior, boundary-feasible when it meets only the cone boundary, strongly infeasible when affine space and cone are positively separated, and weakly infeasible when they are disjoint but have zero distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{SF}&:\ L\cap\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing,\\ \mathrm{BF}&:\ L\cap K\neq\varnothing,\ L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing,\\ \mathrm{SI}&:\ L\cap K=\varnothing,\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0,\\ \mathrm{WI}&:\ L\cap K=\varnothing,\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0.\end{aligned}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Weak infeasibility is infeasibility together with approximate feasibility under arbitrarily small perturbations.
Strong infeasibility is robust infeasibility and admits strict separation of the affine space from the cone.
special_cases_latex: For polyhedral cones, disjoint closed polyhedral sets are positively separated in this affine setting, so weak infeasibility does not arise.
Semidefinite and second-order cone systems can be weakly infeasible.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict feasibility is stable under sufficiently small data perturbations.
Boundary feasibility and weak infeasibility lie on the boundary between robust feasibility and robust infeasibility.
boundary_notes: This status classifies feasibility, not objective boundedness or attainment.
The distance is computed with any fixed Euclidean norm; zero versus positive distance is norm-independent in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly Feasible Right-Hand-Side Stratum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-space and image-space characterizations of strict feasibility for a finite-dimensional conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(b)=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\). Call the system strictly feasible when \(Q(b)\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\). Since linear maps preserve relative interiors of nonempty convex sets, \[A(\operatorname{ri}K)=\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).\] Consequently, \[Q(b)\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\in\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is strictly feasible exactly when its right-hand side lies in the relative interior of the cone of feasible right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\in\operatorname{ri}K\ \text{with}\ Ax=b\iff b\in\operatorname{ri}(A(K))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Feasible Right-Hand-Side Stratum

assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is strictly feasible exactly when \(b\in A(\operatorname{ri}K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior strict feasibility for a finite-dimensional conic linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is in the strictly feasible regime when \[Q\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing,\qquad Q:=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}.\] Equivalently, there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) satisfying \(A\bar x=b\), or \(b\in A(\operatorname{ri}K)\). Relative interior is essential when \(K\) is not full-dimensional; replacing it by the ambient interior would incorrectly classify every feasible point of such a cone as non-strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is strictly feasible when its affine constraints admit a point in the cone's relative interior.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Feasible Conic Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of the Feasible Image Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image-space representation of strict feasibility for a finite-dimensional conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) linear. Then
\[
A(\operatorname{ri}K)=\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).
\]
Consequently, the conic system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is strictly feasible if and only if
\[
b\in\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly feasible right-hand sides form exactly the relative interior of the cone of feasible right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in\operatorname{ri}K\ \text{with}\ Ax=b\iff b\in\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict feasibility of a cone program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict feasibility for the source's conic primal representation, together with its stated invariance under the associated finite reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\inf_x\{c^Tx:Px=p,\ A_i x-b_i\in K^i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is strictly feasible if there exists \(\bar x\) satisfying \(P\bar x=p\) and \(A_i\bar x-b_i\in\operatorname{int}K^i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). In the source's associated formulation, \((\mathrm{Pr})\) is strictly feasible if and only if \((\mathrm{Fin})\) is strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone program is strictly feasible when an equality-feasible point places every cone-inequality slack in the interior of its cone. The source states that this property is unchanged by its associated finite reformulation.
assumptions_latex: Under the section's standing convention, the rows of \(P\) are linearly independent and \(\ker P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\ker A_i=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathrm{Pr})\text{ is strictly feasible}\iff\exists\bar x:\ P\bar x=p,\ A_i\bar x-b_i\in\operatorname{int}K^i\ \forall i;\qquad (\mathrm{Pr})\text{ strictly feasible}\iff(\mathrm{Fin})\text{ strictly feasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and optimality under two-sided strict conic feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conic regularity regime in which both members of a primal–dual pair have interior feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
(P)\quad \inf_x\{c^Tx:Ax-b\in K\},\qquad
(D)\quad \sup_\lambda\{b^T\lambda:A^T\lambda=c,\ \lambda\in K_*\}.
\]
If there exist \(\bar x\) and \(\bar\lambda\) such that
\[
A\bar x-b\in\operatorname{int}K,\qquad
\bar\lambda\in\operatorname{int}K_*,\qquad
A^T\bar\lambda=c,
\]
then both problems attain their optima and their optimal values are equal. Moreover, for every primal–dual feasible pair \((x,\lambda)\),
\[
(x,\lambda)\text{ is primal–dual optimal}
\iff c^Tx=b^T\lambda
\iff \lambda^T(Ax-b)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both sides of a conic primal–dual pair are strictly feasible, both optima are attained and have the same value. A feasible pair is optimal exactly when its duality gap is zero, equivalently when complementary slackness holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ and }D\text{ attain equal optimal values, and }(x,\lambda)\text{ is optimal}\iff c^Tx=b^T\lambda\iff\lambda^T(Ax-b)=0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-feasibility definitions for the primal and dual sides of a conic linear pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\mathring{\mathcal F}_p:=\{\mathbf X:\mathcal A\mathbf X=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf X\in\operatorname{int}K\}

\[
\mathring{\mathcal F}_d:=\{(\mathbf y,\mathbf S):\mathbf y^T\mathcal A+\mathbf S=\mathbf C,\ \mathbf S\in\operatorname{int}(K^*)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-Feasible Right-Hand-Side Stratum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-space and image-space characterizations of boundary feasibility for a finite-dimensional conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(b)=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\). Call the system boundary-feasible when \(Q(b)\neq\varnothing\) but \(Q(b)\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\). Since linear maps preserve relative interiors of nonempty convex sets, \[A(\operatorname{ri}K)=\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).\] Therefore \[Q(b)\neq\varnothing,\ Q(b)\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\in A(K)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(A(K)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary-feasible systems have feasible points but no relative-interior feasible point; their right-hand sides are exactly the feasible image points outside the image cone's relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(b)\neq\varnothing\ \text{and}\ Q(b)\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\iff b\in A(K)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(A(K))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Feasible Right-Hand-Side Stratum

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space, and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Boundary feasibility is characterized by \(b\in A(K)\setminus A(\operatorname{ri}K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility attained only on the relative boundary of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic system is boundary-feasible when it is feasible but not strictly feasible: \[Q:=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing,\qquad Q\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \[b\in A(K)\setminus A(\operatorname{ri}K).\] Consequently every feasible point belongs to the relative boundary \(K\setminus\operatorname{ri}K\). This condition records failure of the usual relative-interior constraint qualification without asserting infeasibility or a duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is boundary-feasible when feasible points exist but every one lies on the cone's relative boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quantitative Strong-Infeasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized separation certificate and exact infeasibility margin for a finite-dimensional equality-form conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) be linear. With the nonnegative dual-cone convention, \[\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K))=\max\{-\langle b,y\rangle:\ \|y\|_*\le 1,\ A^*y\in K^*\}.\] Hence \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is strongly infeasible exactly when this maximum is positive. Any \(y\) satisfying \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) certifies strong infeasibility, and \(-\langle b,y\rangle/\|y\|_*\) is a lower bound on every residual \(\|Ax-b\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong-infeasibility distance equals an optimal normalized separation value, and every strict separator supplies a quantitative residual lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K))>0\) if and only if there exists \(y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quantitative Strong-Infeasibility Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space, and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong infeasibility is equivalent to \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\), or equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K))>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-distance infeasibility for a finite-dimensional conic linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is strongly infeasible when \[\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K)):=\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|>0.\] In finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\). Thus infeasibility persists under every perturbation of \(b\) whose norm is smaller than the positive distance. By strict separation, this regime admits a nonzero \(y\in F\) satisfying \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\), after a positive rescaling if desired.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong infeasibility means the right-hand side has positive distance from the cone's linear image, so sufficiently small perturbations cannot restore feasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong infeasibility of an affine conic system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Consider \(Ax-b\in K\), and write \(L=\operatorname{range}A-b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-cone feasibility; strong infeasibility is measured in the ambient Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(Ax-b\in K\) is strongly infeasible if \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \[\operatorname{dist}(L,K):=\inf_{x\in E,\,k\in K}\|Ax-b-k\|>0.\] Equivalently, the affine space and cone admit strict conic separation: there exists \(y\in K^*\) such that \(A^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle>0\). Such a \(y\) is a finite strong-infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional affine conic system is strongly infeasible when its affine slack space is disjoint from the cone by a strictly positive distance. This is the regime in which a dual-cone vector annihilating the range of \(A\) strictly separates every affine slack from \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq Y\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax-b\in K\) is strongly infeasible precisely when \(\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{range}A-b,K)>0\); equivalently, \(\exists y\in K^*\) with \(A^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: After positive rescaling, the certificate may be normalized by \(\langle b,y\rangle=1\).
The right-hand-side system is not almost solvable: some neighborhood of \(b\) contains no \(b'\) for which \(Ax-b'\in K\) is solvable.
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedral cone, every infeasible affine conic system is strongly infeasible.
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), the certificate is the usual strict Farkas certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strong infeasibility is stable under sufficiently small perturbations of \(b\).
A finite separating certificate exists.
boundary_notes: Mere infeasibility does not imply positive distance for general nonpolyhedral cones.
The distance and strict-separation equivalence stated here uses finite dimensionality and closedness of \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is infeasible. It is weakly infeasible if and only if \[\langle b,y\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in F^*\text{ with }A^*y\in K^*.\] Thus weak infeasibility admits no strict separator \(y\) satisfying \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Weak-Infeasibility Example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional nonclosed semidefinite image producing zero-distance infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \[A\!\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=(a,c).\] Then \[A(K)=\{(a,c):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] For \(b=(0,1)\), one has \(b\notin A(K)\) but \(b\in\overline{A(K)}\). Indeed, the matrices \[X_n=\begin{pmatrix}1/n&1\\1&n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\] satisfy \(A(X_n)=(1/n,1)\to b\). Therefore \(A(X)=b,\ X\succeq0\) is weakly infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection of the two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone misses a boundary point approached by feasible images.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^2\) denotes the cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite two-by-two matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,1)\in\overline{A(\mathbb S_+^2)}\setminus A(\mathbb S_+^2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Weak-Infeasibility Example

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space, and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
The conic feasibility system is \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-distance, unattained conic infeasibility caused by nonclosed image geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is weakly infeasible when it has no feasible point but its residual can be made arbitrarily small: \[b\notin A(K),\qquad \inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0.\] Equivalently, \[b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K).\] Hence there exists a sequence \((x_n)\subset K\) with \(Ax_n\to b\), although no \(x\in K\) satisfies \(Ax=b\). This regime can occur only when the image cone \(A(K)\) is not closed at \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility means no feasible point exists, yet conic points can achieve arbitrarily small residual because the right-hand side lies in the nonattained closure of the image cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification-failure repair system for conic optimization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a conic program with feasible slacks \(S=(b-\operatorname{range}A)\cap K\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone, and suppose \(S\neq\varnothing\) but \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic programs failing a relative-interior constraint qualification; this is an umbrella repair object rather than a single algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A qualification-failure repair system is a tuple \(\mathcal R=(F_{\min},\mathcal E,\widehat D,\bar p)\) such that: \(F_{\min}=\operatorname{face}_K(S)\); \(\mathcal E\) is a finite facial-reduction certificate identifying \(F_{\min}\); \(\widehat D\) is an extended dual over auxiliary certificate variables whose value equals the primal value whenever finite; and \(\bar p=\operatorname{cl}p\) is the closed perturbation-value function. The reduced primal replaces \(K\) by \(F_{\min}\), preserves its feasible set and objective values, and satisfies \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualification-failure repair system packages the minimal-face reduction, its exposing certificates, an extended dual, and closure of the perturbation value. It is required to preserve the original primal feasible points and objective values while expressing the problem relative to the smallest cone face in which strict relative feasibility is restored.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is a repair system only if reduction to \(F_{\min}\) preserves the primal problem and restores relative-interior feasibility, while \(\widehat D\) and \(\bar p\) encode the repaired dual value.
special_cases_latex: If \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\), the trivial repair has \(F_{\min}=K\) and no facial-reduction steps.
immediate_consequences_latex: The repaired formulation separates geometric reduction from value closure and dual lifting.
boundary_notes: This definition does not select a unique facial-reduction sequence or a unique extended dual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial reduction of a conic feasibility system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let \(S=(b-\operatorname{range}A)\cap K\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasible conic systems lacking strict feasibility in their current cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facial-reduction step chooses a nonzero exposing vector \(y\in K^*\) satisfying \(A^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\), and replaces \(K\) by the proper exposed face \[K' = K\cap y^\perp.\] Because every feasible slack \(s=b-Ax\) satisfies \(\langle y,s\rangle=0\), the replacement preserves \(S\). Facial reduction is the finite iteration of such steps until the current face \(F\) satisfies \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly intersects the current cone with hyperplanes exposed by dual-cone vectors that vanish on every feasible slack. Each step preserves feasibility while shrinking the ambient cone, and the process terminates when the feasible slacks meet the relative interior of the remaining face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F_0:=K\). At step \(i\), if \(Q\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i\neq\varnothing\), stop and output \(F_i\). A sequence terminating at the first relatively strictly feasible face outputs \(F_i=F_{\min}\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S=(b-\operatorname{range}A)\cap K\neq\varnothing\), with \(K\) a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible finite-dimensional conic systems; the sequence records successive exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facial-reduction sequence of length \(d\) is a chain \[K=F_0\supsetneq F_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq F_d\] with vectors \(y_i\in F_{i-1}^*\setminus F_{i-1}^{\perp}\) such that \(A^*y_i=0\), \(\langle b,y_i\rangle=0\), and \[F_i=F_{i-1}\cap y_i^\perp\qquad(i=1,\ldots,d).\] It is terminating when \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_d\neq\varnothing\), and it is minimal when no terminating sequence has smaller length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facial-reduction sequence is a strictly descending chain of cone faces. Each face is exposed inside the preceding face by a nontrivial dual vector that annihilates the affine constraint data, so every feasible slack remains in every face. A terminating sequence reaches a face in which relative strict feasibility holds.
assumptions_latex: Every \(y_i\) belongs to the dual of the current face and is nontrivial on that face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data \((F_i,y_i)_{i=1}^d\) form a facial-reduction sequence exactly when the stated orthogonality, dual-cone, and face-update conditions hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For each \(i\), \(S\subseteq F_i\) and \(F_i\) is a proper exposed face of \(F_{i-1}\).
special_cases_latex: A length-zero sequence is terminating precisely when \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended dual formulation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((P)\) be a finite-dimensional conic minimization problem with value \(v_P\), and let its standard dual have feasible set \(D\), objective \(g\), and value \(v_D\leq v_P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic duality repair by finite-dimensional lifting; this defines the structural class, not one particular lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended dual of \((P)\) is a maximization problem \[\widehat v_D=\sup\{\widehat g(z):z\in\widehat D\}\] in an augmented finite-dimensional space, together with a projection \(\pi:\widehat D\to Y\), such that every standard-dual point has a lift preserving objective value, and every extended feasible point gives a valid primal lower bound: \[\{y\in D\}\subseteq\pi(\widehat D),\qquad \widehat g(z)\leq v_P.\] It is value-exact when \(\widehat v_D=v_P\) for every primal instance in its stated class, and attainment-exact when the supremum is attained whenever \(v_P\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended dual augments the standard dual with auxiliary variables and constraints. It must contain value-preserving lifts of ordinary dual feasible points and retain weak duality. Exactness additionally requires its value to equal the primal value, with attainment if that property is claimed.
assumptions_latex: \((P)\) is a finite-dimensional conic optimization problem.
The standard dual is specified with feasible set \(D\) and objective \(g\).
\(\widehat D\), \(\widehat g\), and \(\pi\) are finite-dimensional conic-representable data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted problem is an extended dual when it extends ordinary dual certificates and preserves weak duality; exactness is the additional identity \(\widehat v_D=v_P\).
special_cases_latex: The standard dual itself is a trivial extended dual when no auxiliary variables are introduced.
Facial-reduction and Ramana-type duals are nontrivial extended duals.
immediate_consequences_latex: An exact extended dual can eliminate a standard-dual value gap or nonattainment without changing the primal.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary relaxation with a larger value is not an extended dual unless every feasible point remains a valid lower-bound certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\). Then this feasible set meets \(\operatorname{ri}F\), so replacing \(K\) by \(F\) restores relative-interior feasibility. The associated facial-reduction extended dual is
\[\sup_{y}\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y\in F^*\}.\]
A finite facial-reduction sequence supplies exposing vectors that describe \(F\) and thereby enlarges the ordinary dual feasible representation from \(K^*\) to \(F^*\). Under the assumptions, conic strong duality on \(F\) gives equality with \(p^\star\), together with dual attainment for finite \(p^\star\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be obtained from \(\mathbb S_+^n\) by finitely many facial-reduction steps and be minimal for the affine system \(\mathcal A X=b\). An exact extended dual retains the exposing certificates for those steps as auxiliary variables and has terminal optimization problem

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p:U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be the convex perturbation-value function of a finite-dimensional convex program, with nominal parameter \(0\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation duality; the family repairs nonclosed value behavior at the nominal parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closure-regularization repair family for \(p\) is a collection \(\{p_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I}\) of proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions or regularized value functions such that \[p_\alpha\leq p,\qquad \sup_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha(u)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(u)\] at every parameter in the stated domain, in particular at \(u=0\). The repaired nominal value is \(\bar v=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\), which equals the value represented by the closed dual object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure-regularization repair family replaces a possibly nonclosed perturbation value by closed convex minorants or regularized value functions whose supremum is its lower-semicontinuous closure. The repaired nominal value is the closed value at zero.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is a closure repair when its pointwise supremum is \(\operatorname{cl}p\), with repaired value \((\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{cl}p=p^{**}\) for proper convex \(p\).
special_cases_latex: The singleton family \(\{\operatorname{cl}p\}\) is the canonical closure repair.
Penalty or proximal regularizations can form approximating subfamilies when their values increase to \(\operatorname{cl}p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the closed dual value by evaluating the lower-semicontinuous convex closure of \(v\) at the reference perturbation:
\[d_{\mathrm{cl}}:=v^{**}(0)=(\operatorname{cl}v)(0)=\liminf_{u\to0}v(u).\]
Consequently \(d_{\mathrm{cl}}\leq v(0)\). The closure gap is
\[v(0)-d_{\mathrm{cl}}=v(0)-v^{**}(0),\]
and it vanishes if and only if \(v\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\). Thus dual-value closure repairs a value discrepancy by replacing the possibly nonclosed value at \(0\) with the value determined by nearby perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed dual value is the biconjugate value at zero, equal to the lower limit of nearby primal values; the closure gap measures failure of lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Value Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed dual value of a convex perturbation problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:U\rightrightarrows\overline{\mathbb R}^{X}\) be a closed convex bifunction for a finite-dimensional convex program, and define \(p(u)=\inf_x(Fu)(x)\). Let \(F^*\) be its adjoint bifunction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex perturbation duality at the nominal parameter \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual-value closure at the nominal parameter is \[v_{\mathrm{cl}}:=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)=p^{**}(0).\] For the dual program associated with \(F^*\), this closed value is \[v_{\mathrm{cl}}=\sup_{u^*}(F^*0)(u^*).\] Thus dual-value closure replaces the possibly nonclosed primal perturbation value \(p(0)\) by the value obtained from the closure of \(\operatorname{epi}p\) at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-value closure is the lower-semicontinuous closed perturbation value at the nominal parameter. For a closed convex bifunction it equals the associated dual supremum, while the unclosed primal value can be larger.
assumptions_latex: The primal and parameter spaces are finite-dimensional.
The conjugacy conventions defining \(F^*\) are those of convex bifunction duality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{cl}}=\liminf_{u\to0}p(u)\) when the lower-semicontinuous envelope is evaluated sequentially in finite dimensions.
Zero duality gap holds at the value level exactly when \(p(0)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(p\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\), then \(v_{\mathrm{cl}}=p(0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A value gap is the closure defect \(p(0)-(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\) when both values are finite.
boundary_notes: Value closure alone does not imply attainment of either primal or dual optimization.
The formula relies on closed convex bifunction duality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\varepsilon>0\), define the neighborhood-regularized value
\[v_\varepsilon:=\inf\{v(u):\|u\|\leq\varepsilon\}.\]
The family is monotone nondecreasing as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), and
\[\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}v_\varepsilon=\liminf_{u\to0}v(u)=v^{**}(0).\]
Hence perturbational regularization recovers the closed dual value from optimization problems permitting vanishing constraint perturbations. If \(v\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\), the limit equals \(v(0)\); otherwise it converges to the strictly smaller closed value and exposes the closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing over shrinking perturbation neighborhoods converges to the closed value at zero, revealing whether the original value is lower semicontinuous there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbational regularization of a convex value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p(u)=\inf_x F(x,u)\) be a proper convex perturbation-value function on a finite-dimensional parameter space \(U\), with nominal parameter \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex value functions regularized in the perturbation variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a proper lower-semicontinuous strongly convex function \(r:U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(r(0)=0\), the perturbational regularization with parameter \(\varepsilon>0\) is \[p_\varepsilon(0):=\inf_{u\in U}\left\{p(u)+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}r(u)\right\}.\] More generally, \(p_\varepsilon(v)=\inf_u\{p(u)+\varepsilon^{-1}r(u-v)\}\). The family is exact at the nominal value when \(p_\varepsilon(0)\uparrow(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbational regularization permits a parameter displacement but penalizes its size by an increasingly steep convex penalty. The resulting infimal-convolution values form a closed approximation to the perturbation value, and exactness means convergence to the closed nominal value.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a proper convex extended-real-valued function.
\(r\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, strongly convex, and minimized at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\varepsilon=p\mathbin{\square}(\varepsilon^{-1}r)\), and an exact regularization satisfies \(\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}p_\varepsilon(0)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(r(u)=\tfrac12\|u\|^2\), \(p_\varepsilon\) is the Moreau envelope of \(p\).
special_cases_latex: Constraint-level perturbations use \(p(u)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\leq u\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each regularized value allows nearby parameters while controlling their displacement cost.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns value regularization, not robust optimization against all perturbations.
Convergence to \(p(0)\) itself requires lower semicontinuity at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Gap Multiplier-Nonattainment Diagnostic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional separation of zero duality gap from multiplier existence after qualification failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\{x:x^2\leq0\}\] has value \(0\). Its dual function is \[q(\lambda)=\inf_x(x+\lambda x^2)=-\frac1{4\lambda}\quad(\lambda>0),\qquad q(0)=-\infty.\] Thus \(\sup_{\lambda\geq0}q(\lambda)=0\), but no finite multiplier attains it; stationarity also fails at the unique feasible point \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failed strict feasibility can leave a zero duality gap while destroying multiplier attainment and KKT necessity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal and dual values are both \(0\), but the dual supremum is unattained and no finite KKT multiplier exists.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multiplier for the constraint x squared less than or equal to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Multiplier-Nonattainment Diagnostic

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Gap and Multiplier-Diagnostic Implication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical relation between closure-gap and multiplier diagnostics at a finite reference value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y^*\in\partial v(0)\), then \(u\mapsto v(0)+\langle y^*,u\rangle\) is a continuous affine minorant touching \(v\) at zero. Therefore \[v^{**}(0)=v(0).\] Consequently, \[v(0)>v^{**}(0)\Longrightarrow\partial v(0)=\varnothing.\] The converse fails in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained supporting multiplier rules out a closure gap; missing multipliers can nevertheless coexist with zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(v:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(0)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow v(0)=v^{**}(0)\), but the converse implication need not hold.

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous convex hull value at zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Gap and Multiplier-Diagnostic Implication

assumptions_latex: A convex optimization problem is represented by a proper convex perturbation value function \(v:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
The reference problem has finite value \(v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of closedness at \(0\) diagnoses a value gap, while \(\partial v(0)=\varnothing\) diagnoses absence of a supporting multiplier.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential at the reference perturbation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-function diagnostics separating closure failure from multiplier nonexistence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Qualification failure at the reference perturbation is diagnosed through two distinct predicates. The closure diagnostic is
\[v(0)>v^{**}(0)=\liminf_{u\to0}v(u),\]
equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}v\) is not closed at \((0,v(0))\); this permits a duality gap. The multiplier diagnostic is
\[\partial v(0)=\varnothing,\]
meaning that no continuous affine minorant supports \(v\) at \(0\); this permits nonattainment of the multiplier dual even when \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\). Thus value-gap failure and missing-certificate failure must be tested separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure defect in the value function diagnoses a possible duality gap; an empty subdifferential diagnoses missing multipliers, and either defect may occur without the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification-Failure Diagnostics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the diagnostics container, but no source supports the claimed diagnostic taxonomy or the precise interpretation of epigraph closedness at the reference value and multiplier nonattainment.

assumptions_latex: The proposed repair acts on a convex perturbation model or a finite-dimensional conic formulation.
The original problem may be infeasible, unbounded, nonclosed, or posed in an infinite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No repair is universally exact: applicability requires its own feasibility, boundedness, topology, representability, and termination hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Minimal feasible face when it exists

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of facial, extended-dual, and closure-based repairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Facial reduction requires a nonempty conic feasible set and a usable description of its minimal face \(F\); finite termination is guaranteed by finite-dimensional facial structure, not in general infinite-dimensional cones. Dual-value closure replaces \(v(0)\) by \(v^{**}(0)\), so it does not preserve the original value when \(v(0)>v^{**}(0)\), nor does it by itself produce an attained multiplier. Extended duals are exact only when their auxiliary facial or closure certificates represent the required face or epigraph closure. None of these repairs converts primal infeasibility or unboundedness into a finite attained optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial, closure, and extended-dual repairs require distinct hypotheses and do not automatically cure infeasibility, unboundedness, infinite-dimensional nontermination, or missing attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Repair Applicability Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy of a convex dual certificate map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) parameterize a convex optimization problem, and let \(\mathcal C(\theta)\subseteq Z\) be the set of its valid finite dual, separating, or Kuhn–Tucker certificates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional certificate sets; degeneracy is defined relative to a specified certificate system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The certificate system is nondegenerate at \(\bar\theta\) when \(\mathcal C(\bar\theta)=\{\bar z\}\) and the set-valued map \(\mathcal C\) is locally bounded and continuous at \((\bar\theta,\bar z)\). It is certificate-degenerate when at least one of these properties fails: \[\mathcal C(\bar\theta)=\varnothing,\quad |\mathcal C(\bar\theta)|>1,\quad\text{or}\quad \mathcal C\text{ is not locally bounded or not continuous at }\bar\theta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate degeneracy is failure of existence, uniqueness, or local stability of the chosen certificate set. The definition is relative to a specified multiplier or separating-certificate map, because the same primal feasible set may have different certificate systems under different formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C(\theta)\) is the explicitly specified set of valid certificates for instance \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy occurs exactly when existence, singleton-valuedness, local boundedness, or continuity of \(\mathcal C\) fails at \(\bar\theta\).
special_cases_latex: For Kuhn–Tucker certificates, emptiness is missing-multiplier pathology and nonsingletonness is multiplier nonuniqueness.
immediate_consequences_latex: The classification separates algebraic multiplicity from instability under perturbations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Value Function Without a Finite Multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example separating value-function closedness and zero biconjugate gap from multiplier existence at a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(v:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
v(u)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt{u},&u\ge0,\\+\infty,&u<0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(v\) is proper, closed, and convex, and
\[
v(0)=v^{**}(0)=0,\qquad \partial v(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Indeed, a finite \(\lambda\in\partial v(0)\) would require \(-\sqrt u\ge\lambda u\) for every \(u>0\), equivalently \(\lambda\le-1/\sqrt u\) for every \(u>0\), which no finite \(\lambda\) satisfies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex value function can equal its biconjugate at a boundary point while having no finite supporting multiplier there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(0)=v^{**}(0)=0,\qquad\partial v(0)=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: finite supporting multipliers at the reference perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Value Function Without a Finite Multiplier

assumptions_latex: The convex perturbation value function \(v:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfies \(v(0)\in\mathbb R\).
Lagrange multipliers are identified with continuous subgradients supporting \(v\) at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A missing-multiplier pathology occurs exactly when \(\partial v(0)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the perturbation space
Set of supporting multipliers at zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier nonexistence expressed through the perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multiplier set at the reference perturbation is
\[\partial v(0)=\{\lambda\in Y^*:v(u)\geq v(0)+\langle\lambda,u\rangle\ \text{for every }u\in Y\}.\]
The missing-multiplier pathology is the condition \(\partial v(0)=\varnothing\). It states that the finite primal value admits no continuous supporting affine minorant at the origin and hence no multiplier in \(Y^*\) certifies that value. This condition is logically distinct from a value gap: it may hold even when \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\), particularly when lower semicontinuity does not ensure subdifferentiability in the ambient topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers are supporting subgradients of the value function at zero; the pathology is precisely that this subdifferential is empty despite a finite primal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Multiplier Pathology

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Kuhn–Tucker multiplier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F\) be a convex bifunction with perturbation value \(p(u)=\inf_x(Fu)(x)\), and suppose \(p(0)\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation programs with finite nominal value; no constraint qualification is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The program has a missing-multiplier pathology when its Kuhn–Tucker multiplier set is empty: \[\mathcal M:=-\partial p(0)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there is no finite vector \(u^*\) satisfying \[p(u)\geq p(0)-\langle u^*,u\rangle\qquad\forall u.\] For an ordinary convex program, this means no admissible multiplier vector makes the infimum of the Lagrangian equal to the finite primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing-multiplier pathology occurs when a convex program has a finite optimal value but no finite supporting price vector for its perturbation value at the nominal parameter. In ordinary constrained form, no admissible Lagrange multiplier produces the primal value through the Lagrangian.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a convex bifunction on finite-dimensional spaces.
The nominal optimal value \(p(0)\) is finite.
Multipliers are required to be finite-dimensional vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pathology is \(-\partial p(0)=\varnothing\), equivalently nonexistence of any finite Kuhn–Tucker vector.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a perturbation direction with two-sided marginal value \(-\infty\) under the hypotheses of Corollary 29.1.2.
For an ordinary convex program, no admissible \(\lambda\) satisfies \(\inf_x L(\lambda,x)=p(0)\).
special_cases_latex: Failure of a relative-interior constraint qualification can produce a unique primal optimizer with no multiplier.
immediate_consequences_latex: No primal–multiplier saddle point exists for the specified Lagrangian.
The standard dual cannot attain the primal value at a finite multiplier.
boundary_notes: Nonattainment of the primal optimum is not part of the definition.
A nonempty but unbounded multiplier set is a different pathology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier Uniqueness and Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional singleton characterization for the supporting-multiplier set at an interior domain point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and suppose \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\). Then \(\partial v(0)\ne\varnothing\), and
\[
\partial v(0)=\{\lambda\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\text{ is differentiable at }0,
\]
in which case \(\lambda=\nabla v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of a finite-dimensional convex value function, the supporting multiplier is unique exactly when the value function is differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\partial v(0)|=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\text{ is differentiable at }0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonuniqueness of Kuhn–Tucker multipliers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F\) be a convex bifunction with finite nominal value \(p(0)=\inf_x(F0)(x)\), and define the multiplier set \(\mathcal M=-\partial p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation programs with at least one Kuhn–Tucker multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The program has nonunique-multiplier degeneracy when \[|\mathcal M|>1,\] equivalently, when there exist distinct \(u_1^*,u_2^*\) such that \[p(u)\geq p(0)-\langle u_i^*,u\rangle\qquad\forall u,\quad i=1,2.\] Because \(\mathcal M=-\partial p(0)\), this occurs exactly when the convex perturbation-value function \(p\) is not differentiable at \(0\), provided \(\mathcal M\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier degeneracy by nonuniqueness means that at least two different finite Kuhn–Tucker vectors support the perturbation value at the nominal parameter. For a finite convex value function with a nonempty subdifferential, this is equivalent to nondifferentiability at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a convex bifunction on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal M|>1\iff p\text{ is not differentiable at }0\), under the stated nonemptiness assumption.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The nominal epigraph of \(p\) has at least two distinct supporting hyperplanes with normalized vertical component.
The associated dual optimum set contains at least two multiplier vectors when multiplier–dual-solution correspondence holds.
special_cases_latex: Redundant active constraints can create multiple ordinary Lagrange multiplier vectors.
immediate_consequences_latex: The value function has no unique gradient-based sensitivity vector at the nominal parameter.
The multiplier set is convex and closed, so two distinct multipliers imply a nontrivial multiplier segment.
boundary_notes: Multiple primal optimizers do not by themselves imply multiplier nonuniqueness.
An empty multiplier set is missing-multiplier pathology, not nonunique-multiplier degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Stability of Convex Subgradient Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient regime excluding both multiplier blow-up and invalid finite sequential limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and suppose \(v\) is finite on an open neighborhood of \(0\). Then there are a neighborhood \(V\) of \(0\) and \(M<+\infty\) such that
\[
\|\lambda\|\le M\qquad(u\in V,\ \lambda\in\partial v(u)).
\]
Moreover, if \(u_k\to0\), \(\lambda_k\in\partial v(u_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\to\bar\lambda\), then \(\bar\lambda\in\partial v(0)\). Thus neither multiplier blow-up nor an invalid finite limiting multiplier can occur at an interior point of \(\operatorname{dom}v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local finiteness of a finite-dimensional convex value function makes its supporting multipliers locally bounded and preserves every finite multiplier limit.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is finite on an open neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists V\ni0,\ M<+\infty:\ \sup_{u\in V,\lambda\in\partial v(u)}\|\lambda\|\le M,\quad\text{and}\quad u_k\to0,\ \lambda_k\to\bar\lambda,\ \lambda_k\in\partial v(u_k)\Rightarrow\bar\lambda\in\partial v(0).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Stability of Convex Subgradient Certificates

assumptions_latex: For perturbations \(u\) near \(0\), the multiplier mapping is \(M(u)=\partial v(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate mapping is unstable at \(0\) if it is not locally bounded or not outer semicontinuous there.

notation.meaning: Perturbation sequence converging to the reference problem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential instability of multiplier certificates under vanishing perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unstable certificate pathology at \(0\) occurs if at least one of the following holds: there are \(u_k\to0\) and \(\lambda_k\in M(u_k)\) with \(\|\lambda_k\|\to\infty\); or there are \(u_k\to0\) and \(\lambda_k\to\bar\lambda\) with \(\lambda_k\in M(u_k)\) but \(\bar\lambda\notin M(0)\). The first condition is failure of local boundedness, and the second is failure of outer semicontinuity. Either permits arbitrarily small data perturbations to destroy bounded or convergent multiplier certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificates are unstable when multipliers blow up under vanishing perturbations or when convergent perturbed multipliers limit to an invalid certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Certificate Pathology
